question: Which of the following is a function of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)?

options.B: phagocytoses rod and cone inner segments

explanation: The retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is a single layer of cells that lies between the retina and Bruch's membrane. The RPE is continuous with the pigment epithelium of the ciliary body. Each RPE cell has an apical portion whose villous processes envelop the outer segments of the photoreceptor cells. The lateral surfaces of adjacent RPE cells are joined by tight junctional complexes near the apices. These junctional complexes form the outer retinal blood-ocular barrier. Some of the functions of the RPE include: • Forms the outer blood-ocular barrier • Maintains the subretinal space • Absorbs light • Phagocytoses rod and cone outer segments • Participates in retinal and polyunsaturated fatty acid metabolism (e.g. vitamin A metabolism -- the RPE generates 11-cis-retinaldehyde for the visual cycle) • Heals and forms scar tissue.

question: What layer of the retina shown above contains cells that project to the magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular cell subtypes of the lateral geniculate nucleus?
explanation: Magnocellular, parvocellular, and koniocellular describe three subtypes of neurons located in the lateral geniculate nucleus which receive projections from the ganglion cell layer (layer C) of the retina. Magnocellular "M cells" have large diameter axons, subserve a larger area of the visual field, and are more sensitive to light and motion than parvocellular "P cells." M cells therefore play more of a role in dim lighting conditions. P cells make up about 80% of ganglion cells, are concentrated in the central retina, have smaller-diameter axons, serve a smaller area of the visual field, and play more of a role in color and acuity. Koniocellular ganglion cells were the last cells to be recognized and are thought to play an important role in blue / yellow discrimination. Koniocellular ganglion cells are also believed to be the first affected by glaucoma. This theory ties into using short wavelength automated perimetry (SWAP) to detect early glaucoma. SWAP is essentially analogous to a Humphrey visual field with a blue stimulus on a yellow background. Most modern Humphrey visual field machines can perform SWAP. In this spectral domain OCT slice, layer A is the inner nuclear layer, layer B is the nerve fiber layer, and layer D is the outer nuclear layer.

question: To which of the following structures does the vitreous gel most strongly attach?

options.B: along the major retinal blood vessels
options.A: at the margins of lattice degeneration

question: A 27-year old is struck by a paintball in the right eye while participating in a competitive paintball league. Fortunately, there is no open globe injury and his hyphema and vitreous hemorrhage eventually resolve on their own. However 4 weeks after his initial injury, the patient presents with complaints of a shadow in his superonasal visual field. Which of the following retinal breaks does this patient most likely have given his past history?
explanation: Traumatic retinal breaks are most commonly of the retinal dialysis variety. Retinal dialyses are usually located in the inferotemporal quadrant at the posterior border of the vitreous base.

question: Which of the following structures is involved in constituting the outer blood- ocular barrier?

options.C: nonpigmented epithelium of the ciliary body

explanation: The outer blood-ocular barrier is formed by the junctional complexes between the apices of the retinal pigment epithelial cells. These complexes are also known as "zonulae occludentes." The tight junctions between cells of the nonpigmented epithelium of the ciliary body constitute the blood-aqueous barrier. The tight junctions between the nonfenestrated endothelial cells of the retinal blood vessels constitute the inner retinal-blood barrier.

question: The fovea contains approximately what percentage of total retinal cone photoreceptor cells?
explanation: Approximately 90% of the total population of cone photoceptor cells exist outside of the fovea. Although it is composed of cones (no rods) and processes of Muller cells, the fovea contains only 10% of the total cone photoreceptor cell population in the retina. There are almost no cones in the retinal periphery. The density of cones within the fovea may exceed 140,000 cones/mm2. Cone photoreceptors in the fovea have a 1-to-1 relationship with bipolar cells and retinal ganglion cells which allows the fovea to produce fine visual acuity. These densely- packed cones are predominantly red-green sensitive. In contrast, the region of the retina with the greatest density of rods is extrafoveal in a ring 20 degrees surrounding fixation with a maximum density of approximately 160,000 rods/mm2. Although rod density is high in this area, visual acuity is not as fine because of summation of multiple rod responses in each receptive field (i.e. not a 1-to1 relationship).

question: Which part of the eye acts as a "heat sink" to remove thermal energy from light absorption?
explanation: The choroid has a very rapid blood flow and thus acts as a heat sink to prevent thermal energy buildup from light absorption. In fact, the choroid has the highest blood flow of any human tissue. The pathway of bloodflow in and out of the choroid is: • Blood enters the choroid via the posterior ciliary arteries. • The blood goes from an outer layer of large-caliber choroidal vessels (Haller layer) to an inner layer of smaller-diameter vessels (Sattler layer). This helps to reduce the arterial pressure of the choroid. • The blood then passes further inward through the choriocapillaris. • The blood is then collected in venules into collecting channels of the vortex veins. Most eyes have 4 to 5 vortex veins which exit the eye at or posterior to the equator. • The vortex veins drain into the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins. Other fun facts about this area: • The venous blood exiting the choroid has a very high oxygen tension. Thus, the retinal pigment epithelial cells (which are adjacent to the choroid) have an increased risk of oxidative damage.

question: A representative electroretinogram (ERG) in a normal individual is shown in the figure above. Which retinal structure does the waveform labeled "2" in the figure correspond to?
explanation: The second waveform, which has a positive (upgoing) deflection, is called the "b- wave." It corresponds to the responses of the middle retinal layers containing the bipolar and Muller cells. Extra comment : 1. a-wave: cones and rods (outer PR layer) 2. b-wave: Muller and bipolar cells (inner retina) 3. c-wave: RPE and PRs.

question: Extra comment : 1. a-wave: cones and rods (outer PR layer) 2. b-wave: Muller and bipolar cells (inner retina) 3. c-wave: RPE and PRs Q9-The photoreceptor layer, within which of the following regions of the retina, contains only cones and processes of Muller cells?
explanation: Regions of the macula commonly tested and some associations include the following: 1. Umbo – the center of the foveola. A 150-micron diameter depression observed clinically as the normal light reflex. 2. Foveola – the foveal floor. A 350-micron diameter region representing the “floor” of the fovea. The foveola does not have inner nuclear or ganglion cell layers. The foveola is approximately equal to the foveal vascular zone. 3. Foveal avascular zone (FAZ) – the macular center and fixation point. A region devoid of retinal vessels. 4. Fovea (aka fovea centralis) – A 1,500-micron diameter (approximately 1 disc diameter) region superimposed on the foveola. Contains only cones (no rods) and processes of Muller cells. 5. Parafovea – 500-micron width ring around the fovea. The parafovea has the thickest ganglion cell, inner nuclear, and outer plexiform layers. 6. Perifovea – 1,500 micron width ring around the parafovea. The perifovea is roughly bordered by the optic disc and temporal vascular arcades.

question: What comprises the middle layer of the structure pointed out by the red arrow in the diagram?
explanation: The structure between the choriocapillaris and the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is Bruch's membrane. It is comprised of 5 layers: • basement membrane of the endothelium of the choriocapillaris • outer loose collagenous zone • middle layer of elastic fibers • inner loose collagenous zone • basement membrane of the RPE Breaks in Bruch's membrane can occur spontaneously in conditions such as high myopia or pseudoxanthoma elasticum, or after inflammation or trauma. Such breaks can lead to the development of neovascular membranes.

question: Where does the blood, collected by the structure denoted by the arrow, drain into?
explanation: The arrow is pointing to one of the inferior vortex veins. The majority of eyes have 4 or 5 vortex veins which leave the eye at the equator. The inferior vortex veins drain into the inferior ophthalmic vein (IOV) while the superior vortex veins drain into the superior ophthalmic vein (SOV). The SOV then passes through the superior orbital fissure and drains into the cavernous sinus.

question: Which layer on the above OCT scan differentiates the macula from extra- macular retina histologically?
explanation: The histological macula is defined by 2 or more layers of ganglion cells ("B" in the above OCT). The macula is also known as the "posterior pole" or "area centralis". Extramacular retina contains only 1 layer of ganglion cells on histological sections. Per BCSC retina, the macula is a 5.5 mm area bounded by the optic disc and temporal vascular arcades. The macula is centered 3.0 mm temporal and 0.8 mm inferior to the optic disc center. "A" is the nerve fiber layer; "C" is the inner nuclear layer; and "D" is the outer nuclear layer.

question: The nuclei of the cells that make up the internal limiting membrane (ILM) reside in which layer of the retina shown in this spectral domain OCT?
explanation: The internal limiting membrane (ILM) is usually regarded as the innermost structure of the retina and is made up of footplates of the Muller's cells whose nuclei are located in the inner nuclear layer (along with bipolar cells, horizontal cells, and amacrine cells). In this spectral domain OCT slice, layer A is the inner nuclear layer, layer B is the nerve fiber layer, layer C is the ganglion cell layer, and layer D is the outer nuclear layer.

question: Which of the following is defined histologically as the area of the retina where the inner nuclear layer (INL) and ganglion cell layer (GCL) are absent?
explanation: The foveola is defined histologically as the central floor of the fovea where the INL and GCL are absent. Clinically, the foveola is defined as the area within the fovea, approximately 0.35 mm in diameter, which corresponds to the foveal avascular zone. The macula is defined histologically as the area of the posterior retina with 2 or more ganglion cell layers. The fovea is defined histologically as the depression in the inner retinal surface where the photoreceptor layer consists entirely of cones. The umbo is defined histologically as the central concavity of the floor of the foveola.

explanation: The macula can be defined in different ways; histologically it is the region of the retina where the ganglion cell layer contains 2 or more layers of cells. On a more gross anatomic basis, the macula is considered to be the area of the retina located temporal to the optic nerve and between the superior and inferior temporal arcades. Still others define the macula lutea, or "yellow spot" (a more distinguished name for the macula), as the portion of the posterior retina containing yellow xanthophyll pigment. In this spectral domain OCT slice, layer A is the inner nuclear layer, layer B is the nerve fiber layer, layer C is the ganglion cell layer, and layer D is the outer nuclear layer.

question: Which layer shown on the OCT macula would NOT be affected by chronic glaucomatous degeneration?
explanation: Layer denoted by “D” is the photoreceptor layer. The photoreceptor layer would not be affected in chronic glaucomatous degeneration. Nerve fiber layer (layer "A") (and optic nerve) atrophy occurs with progressive ganglion cell (layer "B") dropout in glaucoma. A condition known as “retrograde maculopathy” has been described in which inner nuclear layer microcysts form, secondary to lesions of the occipital lobe, chiasm and optic nerve. The formation of microcystic cavities in the inner nuclear layer is thought to result from trans-synaptic degeneration and has been described in patients with glaucoma. As a result, glaucomatous atrophy can result in loss of ganglion cells, nerve fiber layer, as well as inner nuclear layer cells with cyst formation. An example patient with transsynaptic retrograde degeneration due to glaucoma is shown below. *This OCT mac was taken from an otherwise healthy, young adult male with severe unilateral pigmentary glaucoma. The OCT mac of the involved eye is remarkable for severe atrophy of the NFL and GCL as well as inner nuclear layer microcystic macular edema due to retrograde maculopathy. The affected eye had severe superior and inferior thinning on the OCT RNFL and advanced field loss on static perimetry. The fellow eye OCT RNFL, OCT mac and HVF were normal. The patient suffered from no central, systemic or other ocular pathology.

question: Which of the following is TRUE of the fovea?

options.D: It is 1.5 mm wide and contains 10% of all cones
options.C: It is 0.35 mm wide and contains 10% of all cones
options.B: It is 1.5 mm wide and contains the majority of all cones
options.A: It is 0.35 mm wide and contains the majority of all cones

explanation: The fovea is the central 1.5 mm of the macula. It is specialized for high spatial acuity and color vision (10% of all cones reside in the fovea). The floor of the fovea is known as the foveola, which has a diameter of 0.35 mm. In the foveola, cones are densely packed. The 150–200 µm depression in the very center of the foveola is known as the umbo, which can act as a sort of concave mirror and provide a lovely overlying light reflex on exam. The parafovea is a 0.5 mm ring around the fovea. Around that is another ring 1.5 mm wide termed the perifovea, the significance of which is it demarcates the anatomic border of the macula. explanation: The blood supply of the choroid is derived from the short posterior ciliary arteries (labeled "D"). There are approximately 20 short posterior ciliary arteries (and 10 short posterior ciliary nerves) that enter the globe in a ring around the optic nerve (labeled "A"). The arterial pressure in the choroidal vasculature is much lower than that arriving via the short posterior ciliary arteries because the blood is rapidly re-distributed by a network of choroidal vessels. The outer layer of (large-diameter) choroidal vessels is called the Haller layer while the inner layer of (smaller-diameter) choroidal vessels is called the Sattler layer. Label "A" corresponds to the optic nerve; "B" to a vortex vein; "C" to the inferior oblique; and "E" to the superior oblique.

question: Which of the following best describes the "macula" if defined histologically?

options.D: the area of the retina without an overlying ganglion cell layer
options.C: the area of the retina with 2 or more ganglion cell layers
options.B: the region of the retina devoid of blood vessels
options.A: portion of the posterior retina containing xanthophyll pigment

explanation: The macula is defined histologically as the area of the posterior retina with ≥ 2 layers of ganglion cells. It is approximately 6 mm in diameter and is centered vertically between the temporal vascular arcades. Answer "A" refers to the "macula lutea"; Answer "B" refers to the "foveal avascular zone."

question: Which of the following best estimates the approximate diameter of the foveal avascular zone (FAZ)?
explanation: The FAZ is the part of the retina that is said to be free of capillaries. Its location is approximately the same as the foveola and is roughly 250 to 600 microns in diameter. The FAZ may increase in size in certain disease states, like diabetic macular ischemia. The foveola itself is defined as the central floor of the fovea where the inner nuclear and ganglion cell layers are absent. The central concavity/floor of the foveola is called the umbo and is partially responsible for the retinal light reflex.

question: Enlargement of the foveal avascular zone (FAZ) beyond what diameter threshold would generally translate into vision loss?
explanation: According to the BCSC Retina book, "evidence of enlargement of the foveal avascular zone greater than 1000 microns in diameter generally means visual loss." Normally FAZ = 250-600 micron.

question: Which layer, shown on the OCT macula above, contains the first-order neuronal cell bodies in the visual pathway?
explanation: Layer denoted by“C” is the inner nuclear layer. The visual pathway extends from the retina to the visual cortex within the occipital lobe of the brain. While photoreceptor cells transduce light into an electrical stimulus, they are not technically considered “neurons” of the visual pathway. Per BCSC retina, the first-order neuron of the visual pathway is the bipolar cell whose cell body resides within the inner nuclear layer of the retina. The second-order neuron of the visual pathway is the ganglion cell whose cell body resides within the ganglion cell layer of the retina (layer "B"). Bipolar cells and ganglion cells synapse in the inner plexiform layer. The axons of ganglion cells traverse the retinal nerve fiber layer (layer "A") until they converge to form the optic nerve. Ganglion cell axons travel from the optic nerve to the optic chiasm where more than half (~55%) decussate to the contralateral optic tract. Next, ganglion cell fibers within the optic tract terminate on third-order neurons whose cell bodies reside within the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN). LGN neuronal axons travel along the optic radiations to terminate within the visual cortex of the occipital lobe of the brain. Note that a portion of the ganglion cell population (so-called “pupillomotor fibers”) do NOT synapse in the LGN but instead, are diverted from the optic tract to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain. These pupillomotor fibers function as part of the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex response pathway. Because of the asymmetric decussation of ganglion cells (including pupillomotor fibers) at the optic chiasm, a lesion of the optic tract causes a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. Some common mnemonics to help remember where cell bodies and synapses between cells are located within the retina: • Inner plexiform synaptic connections: “Cells In a BAG”. Inner plexiform layer --> Bipolar cells, Amacrine cells, and Ganglion cells. • Inner nuclear layer cell bodies: "Big HAM”. Bipolar, Horizontal, Amacrine, and Mueller cells • Outer plexiform synaptic connections: “PHiBers Out”. Photorecepters, horizontal cells, bipolar cells --> Outer plexiform layer.

question: Same explanation in previous question Q24-Which of the following represents the correct order of blood flow through the choroidal circulation?

options.D: Short posterior ciliary arteries → Choriocapillaris → Haller layer → Sattler layer → Vortex veins → Superior and inferior ophthalmic veins
options.C: Short posterior ciliary arteries → Choriocapillaris → Sattler layer → Haller layer → Superior and inferior ophthalmic veins → Vortex veins
options.B: Short posterior ciliary arteries → Haller layer → Sattler layer → Choriocapillaris → Vortex veins → Superior and inferior ophthalmic veins
options.A: Short posterior ciliary arteries → Sattler layer → Haller layer → Choriocapillaris → Vortex veins → Superior and inferior ophthalmic veins

explanation: The choroidal circulation begins with blood entering the posterior ciliary arteries followed by choroidal large-caliber vessels (Haller layer – “H” for Huge calibre) → choroidal small-caliber vessels (Sattler layer – “S” for Small calibre) → choriocapillaris → vortex veins → and finally the superior and inferior ophthalmic veins. Per BCSC retina, retinal tissue ranks among the highest in the body in terms of metabolic rate per gram of tissue. Not surprisingly, the choroid is the site of highest blood flow of any tissue in order to support retinal metabolism as well as remove thermal energy from absorption of light. Due to such high blood flow through the choriocapillaris, RPE cells realize the highest oxygen tension of any tissue in the body and therefore are at high risk of oxidative damage. Some high-yield nerve/artery/vein numbers to memorize: • ~20 Short posterior ciliary ARTERIES • ~10 Short posterior ciliary NERVES • ~2 Long ciliary arteries • ~2 Long ciliary nerves • ~4-7 vortex veins per eye (about 1-2 per quadrant of retina) responsible for draining the uvea (choroid, ciliary body and iris) • One (1) central retinal vein responsible for draining the inner retinal circulation.

question: Angioid streaks are thought to result from increased fragility of which of the following layers on the above optical coherence tomography (OCT)?
explanation: Structure labeled “C” is Bruch membrane. Bruch membrane is composed of 5 sublayers from innermost-to-outermost in the following order: 1. RPE basement membrane 2. Collagenous inner zone 3. Inner layer of elastic fibers 4. Collagenous outer zone 5. Choriocapillaris basement membrane Angioid streaks result from breaks in an otherwise fragile Bruch membrane which expose underlying choroidal vascular layers and may result in vision loss due to acute subretinal hemorrhage and/or choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM) formation. Angioid streaks may be idiopathic or caused by one of several underlying systemic disorders including pseudoexanthoma elasticum (most common identifiable cause), Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, Paget's disease of bone, and sickle cell (and some other hemoglobinopathies). Causes of angioid streaks can be memorized using the well-known “PEPSI” mnemonic where the letter “I” represents idiopathic. Patients with angioid streaks should receive evaluation for the aforementioned conditions. Patients should also be instructed to wear protective eyewear and may require treatments specific for CNVM if present. explanation: The photo above shows a classic chorioretinal coloboma. All colobomas of the globe are caused by incomplete closure of the embryonic fissure in week 5 of development leading to a tear drop shaped tissue defect in one or more ocular structures. Normal closure of the embryonic fissure begins at the equator inferiorly with the process of closure extending anteriorly and posteriorly. Colobomas may be isolated to one region of the eye or large and involve all structures of the eye including the optic nerve, choroid/retina, iris, and ciliary body with dysgenesis of zonules focally leading to lens coloboma. Because the embryonic fissure closes inferiorly, most colobomas occur inferiorly as in our patient (so called "typical" coloboma). The majority of typical colobomas are bilateral as in our patient. Colobomas are by definition present from birth but it is not unusual to find them on examination in adults who have never had an eye exam or were never told that they had a coloboma. Many congenital infections can cause chorioretinal scars including CMV but our patient's pattern of bilateral, tear drop shaped, inferior chorioretinal lesions are classic for coloboma and do not suggest prior infection. Sarcoidosis can cause choroidal granulomas and retinal vasculitis eventually leading to chorioretinal scars but, again, this patient shows no signs of active inflammation and the pattern of the lesions suggest a congenital anomaly requiring no work-up. FA can be used to find an area of active destruction when diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis is suspected. DUSN can lead to extensive chorioretinal scarring, bone spicules, and pigmentary changes but is unilateral and would not be expected to produce an isolated inferior chorioretinal lesion in both eyes. question: Vascularization of the retina is generally complete for the nasal and temporal sides of the retina at what time points of gestation?
explanation: The clinical use of the fact that the nasal retina becomes vascularized (at 36 weeks) before the temporal retina (at 40 weeks) is that if you see (during your ROP exam) that the temporal retina is fully vascularized, then the nasal retina should already be fully vascularized. According to the BCSC Retina book, retinal vascularization is complete in the nasal quadrants at 36 weeks and on the larger temporal side at 40 weeks. Memorize these values! Also remember that the process of retinal vascularization begins at 4-5 months of gestation and involves the outward spread of mesenchymal cells from the optic disc. question: A 1-year-old Caucasian child is being referred to your office by her pediatrician with a diagnosis of leukocoria OU. There is no family history of ocular diseases. The parents have noticed the problem only since the child was 6 months old, but did not seek medical attention. Which of the following attributes most strongly argues AGAINST a diagnosis of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV)?

options.B: lack of family history of ocular diseases

explanation: This child's presentation is concerning for bilateral retinoblastoma (Rb) which occurs in approximately one-third of all Rb children. In contrast to Rb, 90% of cases of persistent fetal vasculature (PFV) are unilateral. PFV is a spontaneous condition, present at birth, and there is typically no family history. Males and females are equally affected. Persistent fetal vasculature is the term that has replaced the condition referred to as "persistent hyperplastic primary vitreous" (PHPV). It is considered the most common cause of a unilateral congenital cataract. PFV's clinical manifestations can be quite varied, ranging from mild cases presenting with prominent hyaloid vessel remnants and large Mittendorf dots, to severe cases with progressive angle closure glaucoma, tractional retinal detachment, and cataract formation. Most PFV eyes are microphthalmic compared to the normal fellow eye, which is important since Rb rarely occurs in microphthalmic eyes. Another classic finding (i.e. typically found on board exams) of PFV is elongated ciliary processes that are visible through a dilated pupil. Management of PFV is difficult in severe cases and typically consists of early cataract extraction, membrane excision via vitreoretinal approaches, contact lens wear, and aggressive amblyopia treatment. explanation: High plus power laser lenses provide wider, less sharp views of the retina that are optimal for broader applications of laser energy such as for panretinal photocoagulation. The view with high power plus lenses is also inverted and the spot size is magnified over the laser setting size (the magnification depends on the specific plus power lens used). In the case of a juxtafoveal CNV, you probably would want to use a negative planoconcave lens to obtain an upright, higher resolution image. The drawback of a negative planoconcave lens is that the viewing area is much smaller, albeit at a much higher resolution. Q-Which of the following laser settings increases the likelihood of developing a choroidal neovascular membrane (CNV) after laser photocoagulation?

question: Which of the following laser settings increases the likelihood of developing a choroidal neovascular membrane (CNV) after laser photocoagulation?
explanation: Small, not large, spot sizes increase the risk of rupture of Bruch's membrane and subsequent CNV. The basic rationale is that any factor that increases the intensity of the laser burn will increase the risk of secondary CNV. Thus, a smaller spot size concentrates the same amount of power into a smaller area (i.e. more intense burn). Other factors that would increase the burn intensity are: • longer burn duration • higher power Frequently, there is the misunderstanding that a shorter duration would result in a higher intensity laser burn. This is not true. Here is an example of how to think about this properly. If you set the laser at 200 mW with a 50 msec duration, that setting will apply that power over every interval of the entire 50 msec. This 200 mW of power is not "spread over" or diluted over 50 msec. Thus, if you increase the duration to 100 msec, the 200 mW of power is applied at every interval over that 100 msec. This results in a higher intensity of laser burn compared to if the duration was shorter at 50 msec. Q-Which of the following colors of light is most absorbed by xanthophyll pigment in the macula?

question: Which of the following colors of light is most absorbed by xanthophyll pigment in the macula?
explanation: Light energy (e.g. laser) is primarily absorbed in those ocular tissues that contain xanthophyll, melanin, or hemoglobin: • Xanthophyll -- readily absorbs blue, but not red or yellow light. • Melanin -- readily absorbs green, yellow, red, and infared wavelengths. • Hemoglobin -- readily absorbs blue, yellow, and green. Minimally absorbs red wavelengths. Thus, you would want to avoid the use of blue wavelengths when performing laser photocoagulation in the macula. explanation: The rationale behind performing focal or grid photocoagulation prior to scatter laser photocoagulation (i.e. PRP) is that the scatter may exacerbate diabetic macular edema. Similarly, focal laser should be performed prior to cataract surgery in cases of clinically significant macular edema to prevent progression of the macular edema. Anti-VEGF agents are another option for this patient which would help both the macular edema and neovascularization, but given the fact that the edema is not center-involving, grid laser is generally preferred. On a practice management level, insurance companies will not reimburse for both focal and scatter lasers on the same day. If done simultaneously, they will reimburse only for the focal/grid laser which has lower RVUs (relative value units). In addition, if a focal is performed within the post-op period (i.e. 90 days) after the PRP, then most insurance companies will not reimburse for the focal laser since it is considered the "lesser" of the two procedures. However, they will pay for a PRP if it is performed within the post-op period of the focal laser. question: You are performing photodynamic therapy (PDT) with verteporfin for a patient with a subfoveal, predominantly classic choroidal neovascular lesion. The patient tells you that he is an avid surfer. For how long should this patient stay out of the sun?
explanation: The most serious side effect of PDT is photosensitivity skin reactions that can lead to serious skin burns. According to the BCSC, this skin burning can be avoided by having the patient minimize sunlight exposure for 5 days after treatment. These reactions occurred in 3.5% of patients in the TAP (Treatment of Age-Related Macular Degeneration with Photodynamic Therapy) study and 0.4% in the Verteporfin in Photodynamic Therapy (VIP) study. Other reported adverse effects of PDT included: • Back, side, and chest pain (2.2-2.5%) which were related to infusion of the drug. • Severe loss of vision within 7 days of treatment (0.7-2.2%). This complication was more common in eyes with choroidal neovascularization lesions that were minimally classic or occult with no classic component. Q-The photo above demonstrates fundus changes following a therapeutic intervention. These changes reflect what type of tissue reaction?

question: The photo above demonstrates fundus changes following a therapeutic intervention. These changes reflect what type of tissue reaction?
explanation: The photograph above demonstrates typical panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) scars. Photoablation, photocoagulation, and photodisruption are all types of laser-tissue interactions. Phototermination is simply a made-up term. Photocoagulation occurs when tissue absorbs light energy delivered by a laser and converts this to heat causing tissue coagulation. Photoablation occurs when laser pulses selectively ablate small areas of tissue without harming adjacent tissue. It is much less destructive than photocoagulation. Excimer lasers use photoablation in corneal refractive procedures because it allows selective ablation of tissue without resulting in damage or subsequent scarring of adjacent corneal tissue. Photodisruption occurs when laser energy is used to rupture or explode tissue. YAG lasers used in posterior capsulotomies and laser iridotomies utilize photodisruption. Q -What is the main advantage of micropulse laser photocoagulation (versus conventional photocoagulation) in the treatment of retinal vascular diseases?

question: What is the main advantage of micropulse laser photocoagulation (versus conventional photocoagulation) in the treatment of retinal vascular diseases?

options.D: Decrease the magnitude of scotomas Laser Therapy for Posterior Segment Diseases
options.C: Higher "duty cycle" of the energy being delivered
options.B: Confinement of heat to the photoreceptors and choriocapillaris
options.A: Improved ability to visualize the laser spots

explanation: In general, laser energy is thought to induce changes in the metabolic activity and gene expression of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells that are adjacent to the burn. In turn, these RPE cells release growth factors and cytokines that control vascular leakage. Conventional laser therapy delivers this required stimulus, but with the side effect of causing permanent destruction to the nearby photoreceptors. This permanent damage can lead to visually-significant scotomas, especially when applied in the macular area. The term, "subthreshold laser therapy," describes the deliverance of laser energy below the threshold of causing permanent tissue [photoreceptor] damage. The main method that is employed to deliver subthreshold laser therapy is micropulse laser, whereby the laser energy is divided into many, short pulses of energy (e.g. 100 to 300 µs duration) with a long pause (e.g. 1700-1900 µs) between pulses. The long pause allows the target tissue to cool enough to prevent permanent damage. Thus, the main benefit of the micropulse laser is the reduction of visually-significant scotomas as a result of less thermal damage to photorecptors. Answer "A" is incorrect since micropulse laser burns are actually not visible even with fluorescein angiography or autofluorescence imaging. This "invisibility" makes it more difficult to titrate treatment and to know what part of the retina has already been treated. Answer "B" is incorrect since the goal of any laser treatment is to confine the laser energy (i.e. heat) to the RPE cells, not the photoreceptors or choriocapillaris. Answer "C" is incorrect since subthreshold lasers actually have a significantly lower "duty cycle" compared to conventional lasers. For example, a micropulse laser can have a duty cycle ~5-10% of a conventional laser. A duty cycle is defined as the amount of time that the laser is actually "on" (i.e. delivering energy). explanation: This patient has extensive neovascularization of the iris and should receive prompt panretinal photocoagulation. Anti-VEGF therapy would also be appropriate in this case, followed by PRP. As she has no thickening on slit-lamp biomicroscopy she does not have CSME (clinically significant macular edema) as defined by the ETDRS (Early-Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study). Remember: CSME is a diagnosis made by slit-lamp biomicroscopy and not by ancillary tests like fluorescein angiography (FA) or OCT. The criteria for treating foveal-involving macular edema have now evolved from the ETDRS to include central-subfield thickness measurements on OCT. This may be used as a surrogate for CSME when deciding on initiating anti-VEGF therapy. Leakage alone on FA however is not an indication for treatment. options.C: Intensive blood glucose control slowed the progression of diabetic retinopathy by 54% compared to conventional management.
options.B: Intensive blood glucose control reduced the risk of developing diabetic retinopathy by 76% compared to conventional management.
options.A: Subjects with type 1 and type 2 diabetes mellitus were randomly assigned to receive intensive blood glucose control or conventional blood glucose management

explanation: The Diabetes Control and Complications Trial (DCCT) was a multicenter, randomized trial of subjects with type 1 diabetes mellitus that were randomly assigned to receive intensive blood glucose control or conventional blood glucose management. Intensive control reduced the risk of developing retinopathy by 76% and slowed the progression of retinopathy by 54%. The risk of neuropathy was reduced by 60% and the risk of nephropathy was reduced by 54% with intensive glucose control. This study established the importance of intensive glucose control in reducing the risk of microvascular complications in type 1 diabetics. Q,Which of the following retinal findings places the eye at highest risk for progressing from preproliferative diabetic retinopathy to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)?

question: Q,Which of the following retinal findings places the eye at highest risk for progressing from preproliferative diabetic retinopathy to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR)?
explanation: The ETDRS (Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study) found that CWS were the LEAST helpful in predicting progression from preproliferative diabetic retinopathy to PDR. The Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy (WESDR) found strong evidence that VB and IRMA are most predictive of the risk of progressing to PDR. The popular ETDRS "4:2:1 rule" in classifying an eye with severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) places the greatest importance on the presence of IRMA (since only one quadrant need be involved). In an eye with severe NPDR, the rate of developing high-risk PDR within 1 year is approximately 17% and within 3 years is approximately 40%. You are examining a 45-year-old patient with a history of type 1 diabetes. A representative fundus photo is shown above. How would you classify his stage of diabetic retinopathy based on this photo alone?

question: You are examining a 45-year-old patient with a history of type 1 diabetes. A representative fundus photo is shown above. How would you classify his stage of diabetic retinopathy based on this photo alone?

options.D: proliferative diabetic retinopathy with high-risk characteristics
options.C: proliferative diabetic retinopathy without high-risk characteristics

explanation: An International Clinical Disease Severity Scale for diabetic retinopathy was established in 2003 and was based on the findings of the Wisconsin Epidemiologic Study of Diabetic Retinopathy (WESDR) and the Early Treatment of Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS). There are 5 stages: • No retinopathy • Mild non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy (NPDR) -- few microaneurysms. • Moderate non-proliferative NPDR -- microaneurysms, intraretinal hemorrhages, or venous beading that do not reach the severity of standard photographs 2A, 6A, and 8A. These "standard photographs" were the ones used by the WESDR fundus photo reading center to judge the severity of retinopathy. • Severe non-proliferative NPDR -- any of the following criteria (but without any neovascularization or vitreous hemorrhage) ("4:2:1 rule") o Intraretinal hemorrhages of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 2A in all 4 quadrants; OR o Venous beading of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 6B in at least 2 quadrants; OR o Intraretinal microvascular abnormalities (IRMA) of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 8A. • Proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) -- presence of any neovascularization, vitreous hemorrhage, or tractional retinal detachment. o PDR with "high-risk characteristics" § Neovascularization of the disc (NVD) of at least the magnitude found in standard photo 10A. This is commonly re-stated as "NVD greater than 1/4 to 1/3 of the disc area"; OR § Any NVD in the presence of preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage; OR § Neovascularization elsewhere (NVE) of at least the magnitude of standard photo 7 in the presence of preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage. § Any neovascularization of the iris or angle. The fundus photo of this patient shows both NVD and NVE (yellow arrows). However, there is no pre-retinal or vitreous hemorrhage and the NVD appears to be less than standard photo 10A. Thus, this eye has PDR without high- risk characteristics. Q-A 48-year-old Hispanic male presents to your clinic for evaluation of sudden decreased vision in the left eye beginning 2 weeks ago. question: Best-corrected visual acuity is measured to be 20/25 OD and HM OS. Tonometry and anterior segment examination are normal for both eyes. Fundus photograph of the right eye is shown above. There is a significant vitreous hemorrhage in the left eye that blocks your view of the fundus. What is the most appropriate next step to care for the patient’s left eye?
explanation: From the question stem, the patient is highly suspicious for proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) of both eyes. The fundus photo of the right eye shows neovascularization of the disc (NVD) as well as neovascularization elsewhere (NVE) along the arcade vessels, thus one can assume that the vitreous hemorrhage (VH) in the left eye is most likely due to proliferative disease, especially in the setting of no recent ocular or head trauma. While all of the answer choices can potentially be possible in-clinic options for PDR, the most appropriate next step for taking care of this patient’s left eye is to perform a B-scan ultrasound (choice C) since there is no clinical view of the posterior segment. Based on presence of NVD and NVE in the right eye, we can assume that PDR is the etiology of the VH in the left eye. However, we must do our due diligence to rule out other ominous posterior segment findings such as a retinal detachment or posterior segment mass (i.e. choroidal hemorrhage, choroidal melanoma, etc.) as these can significantly impact the clinical course. What if the VH is caused by a retinal tear that has now led to a retinal detachment? Once the B-scan has confirmed no other significant posterior pathology, we can proceed based on the assumption that the VH is due to PDR and treat accordingly. Treatment with intravitreal anti-VEGF therapy (choice A) may be appropriate after we confirm with B-scan that the etiology for the VH is not due to other posterior segment disease such as retinal detachment or choroidal mass. Determining which agent (bevacizumab, ranibizumab, or aflibercept) to treat with for this disease is controversial and beyond the scope of the written board exams. Furthermore, on-going anti-VEGF injections versus pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) to manage PDR long-term is also very controversial and beyond the scope of the written boards. Pan-retinal photocoagulation (choice B) would be an appropriate treatment for the patient as a long-term strategy once the VH clears in the left eye. Fluorescein angiography (choice D) is an additional in-office test to confirm and document dye leakage indicative of NVD and NVE in PDR. We would not be able to conduct this imaging study until the VH has cleared in the left eye. Q-On a microscopic level, what is the characteristic vascular change that occurs in diabetic retinopathy?

explanation: The Diabetic Retinopathy Study (DRS) was a multicenter, randomized trial of 1742 subjects with proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) that were randomly assigned to receive panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) or observation. This study demonstrated that PRP reduced the risk of severe visual loss by 50% or more in subjects with high-risk PDR. High-risk PDR was defined in this study according to: (1) eyes with new vessels and preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage; and (2) eyes with new vessels on or within one disc diameter of the optic disc (NVD) equaling or exceeding 1/4 to 1/3 disc area in extent in the absence of preretinal or vitreous hemorrhage. PRP technique was also defined by this study. The DRS established PRP as the standard of care for high-risk PDR during this time period.The Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) evaluated the effects of aspirin on diabetic retinopathy. explanation: The DRVS clearly showed a benefit of early vitrectomy for type 1 diabetics with severe vision loss from a severe VH. Specifically, this study found that early vitrectomy increased the chance of 20/40 vision from 12% to 36% in type 1 diabetics. There was no clear benefit in type 2 diabetics. Though the DRVS provided valuable data, most vitreoretinal surgeons will perform early surgery also for type 2 diabetics with severe VH given the improvement in vitreoretinal surgical techniques, especially the routine use of concomitant endolaser during the procedure. options.D: In non-center involving diabetic macular edema, the most vision is gained by a combination of monthly intravitreal ranibizumab plus macular laser
options.C: If the edema is more severe prior to treatment, then macular laser results in the best visual gain
options.B: Macular focal/grid laser is more effective if the leakage is focal as opposed to diffuse
options.A: there were similar gains in vision for pseudophakes treated with monthly intravitreal ranibizumab and macular laser as compared with triamcinolone and macular laser

explanation: The photographs demonstrate center-involving diabetic macular edema. The Diabetic Retinopathy Clinical Research network (DRCR.net) protocol I had four arms: (1) sham injection + prompt laser; (2) ranibizumab 0.5 mg + prompt laser; (3) ranibizumab 0.5 mg + delayed laser; (4) triamcinolone 4 mg + prompt laser.1 The best vision results at the primary endpoint (i.e. at 52 weeks) were from the two groups of ranibizumab plus laser. In other words, these ranibizumab + laser groups did better than the previous gold standard of macular laser alone. The subgroup that differed was pseudophakic eyes. Pseudophakic patients gained equivalent vision in the ranibizumab/laser groups as the triamcinolone/laser group. However, the triamcinolone group had a much higher incidence of glaucoma. A subgroup analysis demonstrated that the amount of initial edema did not alter the overall result. Also, the vision gain was similar whether the treating physician felt that the leakage was focal or diffuse. The trial only included subjects with center- involving edema and as such cannot be applied to patients without center-involving edema. options.C: Aspirin treatment was found to alter the course of diabetic retinopathy in subjects with clinically significant diabetic macular edema (CSDME).
options.B: The study defined clinically significant diabetic macular edema (CSDME) according to stereo contact lens biomicroscopy or stereo photography.
options.A: The study compared focal argon photocoagulation with observation in subjects with diabetic macular edema.

explanation: The Early Treatment Diabetic Retinopathy Study (ETDRS) was a multicenter, randomized trial of 2,244 subjects with diabetic macular edema that were randomly assigned to receive focal argon photocoagulation or observation. This study demonstrated that focal photocoagulation of clinically significant diabetic macular edema (CSDME) substantially reduced the risk of visual loss by 50% (Report 1). Laser treatment also increased the chance of visual improvement, decreased the frequency of persistent macular edema, and caused minimal visual field loss. CSDME, determined according to stereo contact lens biomicroscopy or stereo photography, was defined by this study as well as focal laser technique (Report 2). The researchers concluded that all eyes with CSDME should be considered for focal photocoagulation. The ETDRS also found that aspirin treatment did not alter the course of diabetic retinopathy (Report 8). The ETDRS established focal argon photocoagulation as the standard of care for the treatment of CSDME during that time period (i.e. before the advent of anti-VEGF injections as used in the RESTORE study). question: Which of the following would be an indication for early vitrectomy?

options.C: Poor vision in the opposite eye
options.B: Extramacular tractional retinal detachment on B-scan ultrasonography

explanation: The patient is presenting with new vitreous hemorrhage in the left eye, most likely due to proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR). The Diabetic Retinopathy Vitrectomy Study (DRVS) studied the use of vitrectomy in PDR patients. Patients with severe vision loss (5/200 or less) from vitreous hemorrhage and a diagnosis of type 1 DM had better visual outcomes with early vitrectomy versus delayed vitrectomy. However, this advantage was not found in patients with type 2 DM. Therefore, it is reasonable to observe these patients for 4-6 weeks before considering vitrectomy. Other indications for earlier vitrectomy include poor visual acuity in the fellow eye, or ultrasound evidence of a rhegmatogenous detachment or tractional detachment involving the macula. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice "A"). The DRVS also studied early vitrectomy in patients with advanced PDR without vitreous hemorrhage. Patients with severe, active PDR had better visual outcomes with early vitrectomy and vitrectomy was more beneficial with increasing severity of neovascularization. Previous PRP increased the chance of good vision. Patients with complete prior PRP who present with vitreous hemorrhage secondary to PDR can therefore likely be observed for a greater period of time. • (Choice "B"). Patients with dense vitreous hemorrhage obscuring fundus examination should be monitored with B-scan ultrasonography to ensure there is no macula involving tractional detachment or rhegmatogenous detachment that would require prompt intervention. Extramacular tractional retinal detachments can be observed. • (Choice "D"). The DRVS did not show a benefit for early vitrectomy in PDR type II DM patients with severe vitreous hemorrhage. explanation: The finding shown is asteroid hyalosis, a degenerative disease due to the development of yellow-white disc shaped bodies (“asteroid bodies”) composed of calcium-containing phospholipids within the collagen matrix of the normal vitreous. The cause is unknown, and the majority of patients have unilateral findings. Patients are usually greater than 50-years-old and a link between hypertension and diabetes has been established. Initially, asteroid bodies develop around retinal blood vessels, but may become so extensive that visualization of the fundus is not possible. Despite this, visual acuity is usually only minimally affected. Fluorescein angiography is one imaging modality that can typically bypass the opacities if posterior pathology is suspected and needs to be characterized or monitored. Abnormal vitreoretinal adhesions such as vitreoschisis are well documented in this condition. Even in the presence of a PVD, residual vitreoretinal adhesions are likely and should be expected if patients undergo vitrectomy. Patients rarely require treatment in the form of vitrectomy, however, as they are typically asymptomatic. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice A): Amyloidosis can lead to accumulation of amyloid material in the ocular structures. It is most often seen in primary familial cases of amyloidosis due to a mutation in the transthyretin gene (a dominantly inherited condition); secondary amyloidosis and nonfamilial cases rarely present with ocular findings. Patients with the familial transthyretin gene mutation additionally have a peripheral neuropathy, amyloid nephropathy, and cardiomyopathy. In the eye, the amyloid material is likely excreted from the retinal vasculature with early findings of retinal sheathing, cotton-wool spots, and localized vitreous veils. As the material accumulates, the vitreous is described as a “cob-web” appearance and visual acuity is decreased. Vitrectomy will restore vision and the material removed will demonstrate birefringence with Congo-red staining. • (Choice C): A monoclonal b-cell population with enlarged nuclei would be concerning for primary vitreoretinal lymphoma (PVRL). PVRL can be thought of as a subset of primary CNS lymphoma (PCNSL). It most often involves the retina, RPE, and vitreous and is frequently of the diffuse large B-cell lymphoma type. When initially presenting in the eye, the disease is a masquerade syndrome that can present with a variety of clinical manifestations and is most frequently misdiagnosed as a posterior uveitis with prominent vitritis. Patients complain of decreased vision and floaters. It is usually a disease of the elderly. PCNSL (disease involving the brain, spinal cord, or meninges) will develop in most patients diagnosed with PVRL, and therefore MRI of the brain is mandatory in any patient with a diagnosis of PVRL. Conversely, 25% of patients with a diagnosis of PCNSL have ocular involvement at time of diagnosis, and approximately 25% of PCNSL patients without initial ocular involvement will develop PVRL. The characteristic lesions of PVRL are sub-RPE sharply defined, yellow- white, tumors (see image). However, the disease can present with many manifestations. For instance, it can simulate a multifocal choroiditis, multiple evanescent white-dot syndrome, an acute retinal necrosis with retinal vasculitis and branch arterial occlusions, optic neuritis, or an isolated vitritis to name a few. Therefore, the diagnosis is difficult. MRI, LP with cytology, and vitrectomy usually all necessary to establish a diagnosis, but can often produce inconclusive results. Treatment involves systemic chemotherapy and/or local therapy with intravitreal methotrexate and rituximab. • (Choice D): Cholesterol-containing crystals describes cholesterolosis, also known as synchysis scintillans, which presents with yellow-white crystalline bodies within the vitreous and anterior chamber. In contrast to asteroid hyalosis, these bodies typically settle inferiorly and are seen in eyes with prior trauma and vitreous hemorrhage. Q-What layer of the retina shown above contains the nuclei of the cells attacked in melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR)?

question: What layer of the retina shown above contains the nuclei of the cells attacked in melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR)?
explanation: MAR is a paraneoplastic, acquired retinal syndrome marked by antibody production to retinal bipolar cells in the inner nuclear layer with evidence of bipolar cell dysfunction on electroretinogram (ERG). The classic ERG findings are that of a "negative ERG" with a near normal A-wave but a markedly diminished B-wave. This same pattern of negative ERG is seen with congenital stationary night blindness and retinoschisis. MAR tends to affect predominately rod function while CAR tends to present with both cone and rod retinal dysfunction (cone > rod) although either can affect rods and/or cones. The vast majority of MAR patients have a known history of melanoma at onset. OCT is generally normal in MAR. Recently investigators have discovered that at least some cases of MAR are due to antibodies to the TRPM1 cation transduction channel on bipolar cells. In this spectral domain OCT slice, layer A is the inner nuclear layer (where the bipolar cells reside), layer B is the nerve fiber layer, layer C is the ganglion cell layer, and layer D is the outer nuclear layer. mnemonic is MAR (melanoma affects rods) and CAR (Cone and Rods), and the ERG looks like an m (one dip, then flat = no b wave). explanation: This patient has central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR), which is a condition which causes idiopathic serous detachments of the retina. It typically presents between ages 35 and 55 with a 3:1 male-female ratio. Type-A personality, hypertension, Cushing syndrome, sleep apnea, psychopharmacologic medication use, corticosteroid use, and pregnancy are all associated with CSCR. The OCT in this case demonstrates a large amount of subretinal fluid, and fluorescein angiography demonstrates a classic “expansile dot” seen in CSCR . While photodynamic therapy (PDT) can be an effective treatment for CSCR, it does carry the risk of choroidal ischemia (answer D) and subsequent atrophy, which occurs in 4% of eyes. Retinal detachment (answer A), cataract progression (answer B), and optic neuropathy (answer C) are not known complications of PDT. Q-Which of the following medications, taken at high dosages, would be most likely to cause a pigmentary retinopathy leading to vision loss after 6 months of use?

question: Which of the following medications, taken at high dosages, would be most likely to cause a pigmentary retinopathy leading to vision loss after 6 months of use?
explanation: The two main phenothiazines are chlorpromazine (brand: Thorazine) and thioridazine (brand: Mellaril) and have been used as antipsychotic agents especially for the treatment of schizophrenia. Only thioridazine (especially at doses >800 mg/day) has been commonly associated with a severe pigmentary retinopathy that can develop even after only week-to-months of high-dose use. The thioridazine-associated retinopathy classically begins as coarse RPE stippling in the posterior pole. Eventually, patchy atrophy of the RPE and choriocapillaris occurs with a characteristic nummular ("coin-like") pattern. In the late stages, thioridazine retinal toxicty can mimic the appearance of choroideremia or Bietti crystalline dystrophy. Visual dysfunction including blurred vision, visual field loss, and night blindness is common and can still progress even if the medication is stopped. In contrast, pigmentary retinopathy is rare with chlorpromazine use. Common ocular side effects of chlorpromazine use includes: pigmentation of the eyelids, interpalpebral conjunctiva, cornea, and anterior lens capsule; as well as anterior and posterior subcapsular cataracts. Hydroxychloroquine toxicity is relatively rare especially with less than 5 years of use. It begins with a subtle granular depigmentation of the paracentral RPE. Eventually, continued exposure to hydroxychloroquine can lead to bilateral atrophic bull's eye maculopathy with paracentral scotomas. In severe cases, it can cause widespread retinal atrophy with severe visual loss. Typical screening tests for hydroxychloroquine toxicity include 10-2 static perimetry (for non-Asians), 24-2 or 30-2 static perimetry (for Asians), and SD-OCT. The earliest finding on OCT is disruption of the parafoveal ellipsoid zone. Q-Which of the following diseases is the leading cause of blindness in the United States for patients aged 20-64 years?

Other relevant facts about hydroxychloroquine and screening for retinal toxicity are that the highest recommended dose is 5 mg/kg/day of total body weight. The recommendations changed from dosing based on ideal body weight to total body weight. explanation: The AAO's 2016 Update on "Recommendations on Screening for Chloroquine and Hydroxychloroquine Retinopathy" recommends getting automated visual fields and spectral-domain OCT for routine primary screening given their wide availability. Specifically, the update recommends: • 10-2 SITA for non-Asian patients • 24-2 or 30-2 SITA for Asian patients. The rationale for this is that toxicity often manifests beyond the macula in this patient demographic. Other helpful screening tests: • Multifocal ERG • Autofluorescence (AF). Increased autofluorescence in parafoveal / extramacular areas may precede areas of thinning on SD-OCT. Late RPE loss appears as an area of reduced AF. Tests not recommended for screening: • Fundus exam and photography. Obviously, if changes are visible on ophthalmoscopy (e.g. Bull's eye maculopathy), then the damage is already very advanced and would have been detected by the other methods much earlier. • Time-domain OCT. • Fluorescein angiography. This test will detect RPE defects, but these are considered late changes. • Full-field ERG. • Amsler grid. • Color vision testing. • Electro-oculogram (EOG). Other clinical pearls from this update include: • The most frequent region of the retina to show early damage is inferotemporal which corresponds with a superonasal field defect. • SD-OCT shows localized thinning of the photoreceptor layers in the parafoveal region in non-Asian eyes or near the arcades in Asian eyes. explanation: The photograph depicts a redidsh-orange vascular tumor that is fed by a dilated, tortuous retinal artery and drained by an engorged vein. These features are classic for a retinal capillary hemangioblastoma. These tumors can occur in both hereditary (autosomal dominant) and sporadic forms. When there are only hemangioblastomas of the eye, the condition is called von Hippel lesions, but when there is also central nervous system and visceral involvement, it is called von Hippel- Lindau syndrome. Vision loss from these lesions can occur from serous retinal detachment or exudate collecting underneath the macula. Vitreous hemorrhage and retinal detachment are other causes of vision loss in von Hippel-Lindau disease. Other key facts regarding VHL syndrome: • Caused by mutation of a gene (VHL - a tumor suppressor gene) on chromosome 3p26. • Autosomal dominant inheritance pattern; high penetrance (varies by mutation) and variable expression. • Central nervous system tumors can include: 20% of VHL patients have hemangioblastomas of the cerebellum, medulla, pons, and spinal cord. • Other findings include: renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytomas, cysts of the kidney/pancreas/liver, cardiac rhabdomyomas. All of the answer choices are possible systemic manifestations of von Hippel-Lindau disease. The primary cause of death from this condition is from cerebellar hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma. Therefore, when this characteristic capillary hemangioma is found, a thorough systemic evaluation should be undertaken. explanation: The most recent recommendations from the American Academy of Ophthalmology state that all patients should keep daily hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) use to ≤ 5.0 mg/kg of real body weight. Thus, the maximum allowed dosage for this patient would be 5 * 60 = 300 mg/day. For patients taking ≤ 5.0 mg/kg/day, the estimated risk of HCQ retinal toxicity is <1% during the first 5 years of treatment and <2% up to 10 years. However, the risk increases to ~20% after 20 years of treatment. The most important risk factors for HCQ retinal toxicity are: • Daily dose >5.0 mg/kg of real body weight. • Duration of use >5 years • Renal disease. HCQ and chloroquine are both cleared to a significant degree by the kidneys. Thus, renal function needs to be monitored closely to prevent unusually high serum levels of these medications. • Tamoxifen use. The risk of HCQ toxicity is increased ~5x with the concomitant use of this breast cancer drug. The mechanism underlying this increased risk is not understood. • Macular disease. Significant central photoreceptor loss could interfere with the tests (e.g. 10-2, SD-OCT) used to screen for HCQ retinal toxicity. Q-A 44-year-old man presents for an annual eye exam. explanation: This child's history and fundus exam are classic for solar retinopathy. Risk factors that predispose an individual to developing this photochemical damage include: (a) younger age; (b) clearer lenses; and (c) drugs that photosensitize the eye like psoralen or tetracycline. Factors that predispose to a slightly lower risk of solar retinopathy include high refractive errors and dark fundus pigmentation. Psoralens are naturally occurring phototoxic compounds that can enter a cell, absorb photons of light, and then produce a photochemical reaction to alter the cell's DNA or other structures. These compounds may be taken orally in the treatment of extensive vitiligo or other skin disorders. Psoralens may be used in conjunction with UVA phototherapy (i.e. "PUVA" -- psoralen UVA) for some skin conditions. The most widely used psoralen in the United states is methoxsalen. Other medications in this class include sildenafil (brand: Viagra), vardenafil (brand: Levitra), and tadalafil (brand: Cialis). Any of these PDE5 inhibitors can cause transient "blue vision" especially when they are taken in higher-than-recommended dosages. These PDE5 inhibitors crossreact with the PDE6 inhibitor which is present in the retina and plays a role in color vision. The blue vision typically lasts 2 to 3 hours and resolves spontaneously. It has been reported to occur in ~3% of men taking sildenafil. Another potential (rare) side effect is the increased incidence of nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION). explanation: The Standard Care vs. Corticosteroid for Retinal Vein Occlusion (SCORE) Study CRVO was a multicenter, randomized, clinical trial of 271 participants that compared the efficacy and safety of 1-mg and 4-mg doses of preservative-free intravitreal triamcinolone with observation for eyes with vision loss associated with macular edema secondary to a perfused central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). After one year, 27 percent of patients in the 1 milligram group and 26 percent of patients in the 4 milligram group experienced a visual gain of three or more lines. Only 7 percent of patients in the observation group experienced a similar visual gain. Patients in the corticosteroid treatment groups were five times more likely to have a substantial visual gain at one year. These results appeared to last up to two years, though the two-year results included a smaller number of patients. Participants who received the 4 milligram dose had the highest rates of cataract formation, cataract surgery, and elevated pressure within the eye, indicating that the 1 milligram dose is safer for patients. This study established intravitreal triamcinolone as an improvement over the previous standard of care observation in the treatment of CRVO-associated macular edema. explanation: The Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion Study (BVOS) demonstrated that grid laser was helpful in increasing the chances of 20/40 vision and a gain in >= 2 lines of vision for patients with chronic (>3 months) macular edema caused by a BRVO. However, this benefit was only seen in patients with intact macular perfusion. In cases of macular non-perfusion, no treatment is indicated. Some key findings of the BVOS: • For BRVO with macular edema, there was spontaenous improvement in ~1/3 of patients after 3 months. • Again, for patients with BRVO with macular edema for >3 months and 20/40 or worse vision, the chances of gaining 2 lines of vision doubled by performing grid laser. • Forty (40) percent of treated eyes had worse than 20/40 and 12% of treated eyes had 20/200 or worse vision after 3 years. These statistics demonstrated that laser treatment of BRVO patients oftentimes did not result in good visual outcomes. • For eyes without neovascularization (NV), eyes treated with sectoral PRP developed significantly less NV than non-treated eyes. • For eyes with NV, eyes treated with sectoral PRP developed significantly less vitreous hemorrhage. This report from the BVOS recommended only performing sectoral PRP after NV developed. Of course, with the advent of anti-VEGF agents, the treatment recommendations of the BVOS are now outdated. For example, according to the BRAVO study published in 2010, this patient may benefit from monthly intravitreal ranibizumab started at the time of presentation. Q-A 22-year-old man presents for a second opinion regarding a longstanding retinal lesion. The patient has noted stable, poor vision in his left eye for as long as he can remember. His past medical history is unremarkable. Best-corrected visual acuity is 20/15 in the right eye and 20/200 in the left eye. The anterior examination demonstrates a clear anterior chamber without cell or flare. The posterior examination of the right eye is normal. The left fundus and late frame fluorescein angiography are shown. Given the likely diagnosis, what further workup is indicated?

question: Given the likely diagnosis, what further workup is indicated?
explanation: The lesion is a retinal cavernous hemangioma. These tumors are hamartomas composed of clusters of thin-walled saccular aneurysms filled with stagnate venous blood and give the appearance of a “cluster of grapes”. They can present within the retina or the optic nerve head. Overlying the lesion, there may be variable amounts of fibrous membranes that can occasionally be associated with vitreous traction and preretinal, or vitreous hemorrhage. The surrounding retinal blood vessels are normal and fluorescein angiography demonstrates delayed filling of the lesion with layering within the saccular aneurysms in the late frame as demonstrated in the photo. Leakage is not seen. Complications such as exudation and hemorrhage are rare. Typically, these lesions are asymptomatic, but can cause loss of vision if present in the macula or if vitreous traction causes vitreous hemorrhage. These tumors do not increase in size and treatment with photocoagulation or cryotherapy to obliterate the tumor is rarely required. Retinal cavernous hemangiomas are usually solitary, sporadic, and unassociated with any systemic condition. There is evidence, however, that some cases can be inherited as an autosomal-dominant neurocutaneous syndrome associated with cerebral, optic pathway, brainstem, and skin cavernous malformations which typically present with neurological manifestations before the age of 25. As such, neuroimaging and a thorough skin examination should be obtained in any patient with a retinal cavernous hemangioma. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice A): Retinal capillary hemangiomas (also known as retinal angiomas, or retinal capillary hemangioblastomas) are congenital, hereditary capillary hamartomas of the retina and optic nerve head. Retinal tumors present as red or pink lesions that are usually associated with arteriovenous (AV) shunting between a dilated tortuous feeding artery and large draining vein. Optic nerve tumors are often flat, not associated with AV shunting, and may be confused for papilledema or a peripapillary choroidal neovascular membrane. Leakage and exudation from these tumors will cause decreased vision. Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner with incomplete penetrance and variable expressivity and is characterized by retinal and CNS angiomas as well as kidney, liver, pancreas, and epididymis angiomas, cysts or adenomas. Other systemic tumors include renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytomas. The diagnosis of a retinal capillary hemangioma requires a systemic workup with genetic testing. Cerebral angiomas and renal cell carcinomas are the leading cause of death in these patients. • (Choice B): Although the majority of retinal cavernous hemangiomas are sporadic, some are associated with a likely autosomal dominant neurocutaneous syndrome with cerebral, optic pathway, brainstem, and skin cavernous malformations. Cerebral hemangiomas can lead to seizures, intracranial hemorrhage, and death. Therefore, neuroimaging should be obtained to rule out this possibility. • (Choice D): Ocular toxocariasis is an inflammatory condition in response to parasitic antigens left by a dead or dying parasite Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati. It typically presents in children or young adults with decreased vision due to a peripheral or macular granuloma. Treatment is with systemic or local corticosteroids. Serum anti-Toxocara IgG titers may aid in the diagnosis but are insensitive. Q-An 8-year boy is brought to your attention for poor vision in the left eye. explanation: FIPTs are different from CWS in that they are at the precapillary level while CWS occur in the superficial radial capillary net. Consequently, FIPTs are deeper, smaller, and more gray than CWS. FIPTs were originally described by Hayreh et al in 1986 and *exclusively occur* in malignant hypertension, unlike CWS which may occur in a variety of ocular diseases. On fluorescein angiogram, FIPTs appear as punctate foci of leakage while CWS typically hypofluoresce due to nonperfusion. Slit-lamp exam shows florid neovascularization of the iris and 1+ flare OS. The patient's past medical history is significant for a past myocardial infarction as well as a stroke. Dilated fundus exam OS shows narrowed retinal arteries, mid-peripheral intraretinal hemorrhages, and dilated retinal veins. question: intraocular pressure (IOP) is 12 mmHg OS. Slit-lamp exam shows florid neovascularization of the iris and 1+ flare OS. The patient's past medical history is significant for a past myocardial infarction as well as a stroke. Dilated fundus exam OS shows narrowed retinal arteries, mid-peripheral intraretinal hemorrhages, and dilated retinal veins. Besides a systemic workup, which of the following should you promptly perform?
explanation: This patient's history of subacute vision loss, iris neovascularization, anterior chamber inflammation, and fundus findings (i.e. narrowed arteries, dilated veins, mid-peripheral intraretinal hemorrhages) are most consistent with "ocular ischemic syndrome." This disease entity is caused by chronic, severe carotid obstruction. Because the patient has florid neovascularization of the iris, prompt panretinal photocoagulation (PRP) should be performed. The patient also requires testing with carotid artery imaging. The decision to perform carotid surgery is based on a number of factors including (among others) the degree of stenosis and other comorbid conditions and is generally not made by the ophthalmologist. In some ways this question is tricky but it simulates standardized tests well. Many test takers recognize that this patient has ocular ischemia and want to treat both the eye (PRP) and appropriately address carotid disease. Ocular ischemia can occur from stenosis anywhere along the path from the common carotid to the ophthalmic artery. Not everyone with ocular ischemia syndrome will have a stenosis amenable to intervention and ultimately it is vascular surgery's decision on what intervention would be indicated. options.C: Combined scleral buckle with pars plana vitrectomy

explanation: Of the available answer choices, pars plana vitrectomy (choice D) is the best option to repair the retinal detachment. Observation (choice A) is not indicated as the retinal detachment needs surgical intervention. Placing a scleral buckle (choices B and C) in eyes of patients with sickle cell disease is not recommended due to concern for causing anterior segment ischemia. Other factors known to increase the risk of anterior segment ischemia after RD repair in these patients include: • detachment of extraocular muscles • use of local anesthesia with epinephrine • overzealous photocoagulation or cryopexy • inadequate patient hydration • inadequate patient oxygenation. explanation: This patient presents with an acute branch retinal artery occlusion (BRAO), bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, and encephalopathy. These findings constitute the clinical triad of Susac syndrome. Susac syndrome is a rare disorder with a female to male predilection of 3 to 1. The typical age at diagnosis is in young adults 20-40 years old. As of present, the exact cause of Susac syndrome is not known, but it is hypothesized to be an immune- mediated injury involving the endothelium of the retina, cochlea and cerebral vasculature. The BRAO that occurs in Susac syndrome can occur at any time during the course of the disease. Its negative effect on vision varies since it can affect just small, peripheral retinal areas, or much larger areas of the macula. Yellowish-white retinal wall "Gass plaques" can be found in this disease and are often found at sites other than arteriolar bifurcations (unlike Hollenhorst plaques). The hearing loss in this disease is typically bilateral, asymmetric, and sensorineural. It also can vary from mild/insidious to severe/acute. Unfortunately, this hearing loss is typically permanent. The encephalopathy in Susac syndrome can manifest with headache (often confused with migraine), confusion, memory problems, ataxia, and personality changes. As of present, there is no standard treatment regimen for Susac syndrome. However, most experts start with intravenous methylprednisolone. Other alternative and adjunctive treatments include: intravenous immunoglobulin (*after* 1 month of oral prednisone), cyclosporine, cyclophosphamide, methotrexate, mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, plasmapheresis, infliximab, and etanercept. Lastly, though there are anecdotal reports of anterior chamber paracentesis and oral acetazolamide helping reverse retinal arterial occlusions, they are far from proven. The blood supply preserving this woman's central acuity is a branch most directly from which artery?

question: Your exam is significant for the findings seen above. A fluorescein angiogram (FA) is performed (frame at 25 seconds shown above). The blood supply preserving this woman's central acuity is a branch most directly from which artery?
explanation: The fundus photo shows retinal whitening but with preservation of perfusion in the foveal area. The corresponding FA shows absence of dye in the majority of the retinal blood vessels except for a few vessels feeding the fovea. This presentation is consistent with a cilioretinal-sparing central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The blood supply to the inner layers of the retina is typically derived entirely from the central retinal artery (CRA). The exception is that approximately 15-30% of eyes have a cilioretinal artery which is a branch most directly from the posterior ciliary arteries (PCAs). The CRA, PCAs, and lacrimal artery are branches of the ophthalmic artery. Most cases of CRAO are visually-devastating with greater than two-thirds of cases having visual acuity of worse than 20/400. The majority of CRAO cases associated with good central visual acuity are those with a patent cilioretinal artery. Vision of NLP typically does not occur in CRAO, but can occur with simultaneous choroidal infarction (e.g. ophthalmic artery occlusion).
