options.D: The extent of macular exudate formation
options.A: The formation or absence of epiretinal membrane

explanation: All of the answer choices listed above are reasons for visual loss following branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) (pictured above in the fundus montage of a right eye). The extent of capillary nonperfusion, however, is by far the most important indicator of visual prognosis in BRVO. For this reason (among other reasons), fluorescein angiography is helpful in evaluation of BRVO. Likewise, it makes sense that the area of retinal ischemia is also the most important predictor of subsequent neovascularization. Q-A 48-year-old man presents for sudden onset, painless vision loss in the left eye for the past two days. Past medical history is significant for hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and coronary artery disease. The patient noted waking up to near total loss of vision in the left eye, but denies headaches, eye pain, or changes in the right eye. V ision is 20/20 OD and 20/400 OS. Fundus examination and late-frame fluorescein angiography are shown in the image. Which of the following is the most common etiology of the patient’s disease?

question: Which of the following is the most common etiology of the patient’s disease?

options.A: Reduced blood flow from carotid artery obstruction

explanation: The patient is presenting with a central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO). The most common cause of a CRAO is embolic, although vascular narrowing, thrombosis, arterial spasm, and reduced blood flow via carotid/ophthalmic artery obstruction, decreased systemic blood pressure, or elevated intraocular pressure can all lead to occlusive retinal arterial disease. The most common etiology of emboli is from ulcerated atheromatous plaques of the carotid artery, followed by cardiac valvular disease. Patients with an embolic CRAO typically experience sudden, painless vision loss that may be preceded by episodes of amaurosis fugax. Ocular manifestations include widespread ischemic whitening of the inner retina most prominent in the posterior pole with sparing of the fovea (“cherry-red spot”). The narrowest part of the central retinal artery is where it perforates the dural sheath of the optic nerve and emboli here will not be visualized on ophthalmic examination. Three major types of emboli occur: 1. Platelet-fibrin: gray-white, elongated plaques associated with large-vessel arteriosclerosis. 2. Cholesterol (Hollenhorst): yellow globules associated with carotid artery disease. 3. Calcific: solid, white plaques associated with cardiac valvular disease Both platelet-fibrin and cholesterol emboli are soft and become fragmented easily. Additionally, during an acute obstruction, collateral flow can develop. As such, fluorescein angiography (FA) will rarely show complete absence of arterial flow. Rather, it will demonstrate a significant flow reduction which will continue to be depressed even after obstruction is relieved due to collapse of the capillary bed by an ischemic and swollen inner retina. Typically, the retinal whitening resolves several weeks following the event, but flow usually is still reduced likely due to loss of the capillary bed in the remaining necrotic inner retina. Visual prognosis is dependent on the duration of obstruction but is generally poor. There is no proven treatment for CRAO, and patients should emergently be worked up for sources of emboli with evaluation of the carotids and heart for secondary prevention of future embolic events. In patients in which giant cell arteritis (GCA) is a concern, an erythrocyte sedimentation rate and/or C-reactive protein should be measured. WRONG ANSWERS: A-C: The most common cause of a CRAO is embolic, although vascular narrowing, thrombosis, arterial spasm, and reduced blood flow via carotid/ophthalmic artery obstruction, decreased systemic blood pressure, or elevated intraocular pressure can all lead to occlusive retinal arterial disease. question: You are examining a 33-year old African American man with complaints of new- onset of "haze" in the right eye. There is a large frond of "sea fan" neovascularization (NV) also located inferiorly. Which of the following represents the most accepted (classic) management for this patient?

options.D: photocoagulation to close feeder vessels to the neovascular frond
options.C: anti-VEGF agent to induce regression of NV
options.B: low-intensity photocoagulation to the ischemic peripheral retina
options.A: pars plana vitrectomy with removal of VH and endolaser

explanation: Low-intensity photocoagulation to the peripheral ischemic retina may cause regression of the NV and decrease the chance of recurring VH. Photocoagulation of the feeder vessels is *not* recommended because this may cause retinal breaks, breaks in Bruch's membrane, and possible choroidal neovascularization. Vitrectomy is not indicated at this time since the VH is small and may resolve on its own. Currently, there have been only two letters to the editor regarding the efficacy of intravitreal bevacizumab for proliferative sickle cell retinopathy.1,2 As such, this modality is currently NOT the most accepted course of treatment. Q-Which of the following ancillary tests can be helpful in distinguishing between a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) and carotid occlusive disease?

question: Which of the following ancillary tests can be helpful in distinguishing between a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) and carotid occlusive disease?
explanation: Ophthalmodynamometry can be used to measure retinal artery pressure. It will show a normal artery pressure in CRVO but a low artery pressure in carotid occlusive disease. As an aside, fluorophotometry can be used to measure the rate of aqueous humor formation. This procedure involves giving fluorescein either topically or systemically and measuring the decline of concentration of fluorescein in the anterior chamber by optical means. explanation: The late phase angiogram shows the classic petalloid pattern of fluorescein leakage consistent with cystoid macular edema (CME). The OCT findings, which show cystic areas of low reflectivity, are classic for the diagnosis. CME is caused by abnormal perifoveal retinal capillary permeability and can occur in many conditions such as: • post-intraocular surgery (e.g. cataract surgery; where it is called Irvine- Gass syndrome) • diabetic retinpathy • branch or central retinal vein occlusion • any type of uveitis (especially pars planitis) • panretinal photocoagulation • retinitis pigmentosa • subretinal disease processes (e.g. choroidal neovascularization) • niacin supplementation Post-cataract surgery CME typically occurs 6-10 weeks postoperatively. In uncomplicated cataract surgery, there is a high rate of spontaneous resolution over the course of 6 months, but most clinicians will treat to hasten its resolution especially if the patient is symptomatic. Typical management starts with topical corticosteroids and NSAIDs (e.g. bromfenac). If the CME is unresponsive to topical treatment, then periocular (e.g. subTenon Kenalog®) or intravitreal (e.g. Triesence®) injection of steroid preparations are commonly employed. Intravitreal (not subconjunctival) anti-VEGF agents (e.g. ranibizumab) are occasionally employed for the treatment for pseudophakic CME. Subconjunctival and topical anti-VEGF agents (e.g. bevacizumab) are occasionally used to induce regression of corneal neovascularization in the setting of high-risk corneal grafts. If the cataract surgery was complicated by vitreous loss or iris prolapse, then these anatomical issues are addressed. For example, a YAG vitreolysis can be performed to break apart any vitreous strands adherent to the cornea (i.e. causing traction). If there is iris incarcerated in the wound, this tissue can be reposited back into the eye to resolve any persistent inflammation that could be contributing to chronic CME. Q-A 35-year-old Caucasian female presents with multiple subjective paracentral scotomas just superior to fixation in the left eye for 1 week. She is otherwise healthy. Visual acuity was 20/20 OD and 20/30 OS. Both pupils reacted well to light and there was no APD. Exam and testing is shown in the figure. Optos wide angle color fundus photo is shown top left, fundus autofluorescence top middle, and infrared (IR) image top right. A spectral domain OCT slice taken horizontally through the macular lesions seen on IR imaging is shown in the bottom panel. What is the pathophysiology thought to underlie this diagnosis?

question: What is the pathophysiology thought to underlie this diagnosis?

options.B: Ischemia of the inner retinal capillary bed

explanation: This is a classic example of a relatively newly described diagnosis, paracentral acute middle maculopathy (PAMM) which most experts believe to be a variant of acute macular neuroretinopathy (AMN). Both are thought to be caused by retinal ischemia although AMN typically involves the deeper portions of the retina (e.g. the ellipsoid region) while the aptly named PAMM results in middle retinal lesions caused by ischemia of the deep retinal capillary bed just deep to the inner nuclear layer. AMN is an exceedingly rare disease initially described in 1975. This disease tends to affect females (approximately 85%) in their reproductive years (mean age 27). The etiology remains unknown but reports are published of associated oral contraceptive use, preceding viral illness, and recent use of stimulants such as epinephrine or ephedrine. Both AMN and PAMM are clinical diagnoses marked by the presence of one or more reddish-brown central macular round or “wedge shaped” lesions that correlate precisely to the location of the patients’ paracentral relative scotomas. Spectral domain OCT (SD-OCT) and infrared (IR) fundus photographs help immensely with diagnosis of both AMN and PAMM. You can see in this example that the lesions exhibited on SD-OCT and IR imaging (used for fundus visualization during OCT image capture) are not clearly seen on the fundus exam nor on fundus autofluorescence images. In some cases, however, the lesions may be seen on fundoscopy. Q-Which of the following is FALSE regarding the "The Standard Care vs. Corticosteroid for Retinal Vein Occlusion (SCORE) Study" ?

question: Corticosteroid for Retinal Vein Occlusion (SCORE) Study" ?

options.D: The researchers concluded that intravitreal triamcinolone should replace laser as the standard of care for retinal vein occlusion-associated macular edema.
options.C: Study subjects that received intravitreal triamcinolone were more likely to develop cataracts than subjects that received laser photocoagulation.
options.B: The study evaluated the effects of intravitreal triamcinolone in subjects with branch retinal vein occlusions.
options.A: The study evaluated the effects of intravitreal triamcinolone in subjects with central retinal vein occlusions.

explanation: The Standard Care vs. Corticosteroid for Retinal Vein Occlusion (SCORE) Study evaluated both central retinal vein occlusions and branch retinal vein occlusions. SCORE CRVO was a multicenter, randomized, clinical trial of 271 participants that compared the efficacy and safety of 1-mg and 4-mg doses of preservative- free intravitreal triamcinolone with observation for eyes with vision loss associated with macular edema secondary to a perfused central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). After one year, 27 percent of patients in the 1 milligram group and 26 percent of patients in the 4 milligram group experienced a visual gain of three or more lines. Only 7 percent of patients in the observation group experienced a similar visual gain. Patients in the corticosteroid treatment groups were five times more likely to have a substantial visual gain at one year. These results appeared to last up to two years, though the two-year results included a smaller number of patients. Participants who received the 4 milligram dose had the highest rates of cataract formation, cataract surgery, and elevated pressure within the eye, indicating that the 1 milligram dose is safer for patients. This study established intravitreal triamcinolone as an improvement over the previous standard of care observation in the treatment of CRVO-associated macular edema. SCORE BRVO was a multicenter, randomized clinical trial of 411 participants that compared the efficacy and safety of 1-mg and 4-mg doses of preservative-free intravitreal triamcinolone with standard care (grid photocoagulation in eyes without dense macular hemorrhage and deferral of photocoagulation until hemorrhage clears in eyes with dense macular hemorrhage) for eyes with vision loss associated with macular edema secondary to branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO). After one year, 29 percent of patients in the laser treatment group, 26 percent of patients in the 1 milligram corticosteroid injection group, and 27 percent of patients in the 4 milligram injection group experienced a visual gain of three or more lines. These results appeared to last up to three years, though the three-year results included a smaller number of patients. However, patients who received either dose of corticosteroid medication were more likely to develop a cataract or experience elevated pressure within the eye than patients who received laser treatment. Also, between one and two years after enrollment in the study, patients in the 4 milligram group underwent more cataract surgeries than patients in the other groups. The researchers recommended that grid photocoagulation remain the standard of care and the benchmark against which other treatments are compared in future clinical trials. explanation: The fundus photograph shows the diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages that are typical for a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). There are two main subtypes of CRVO: non-ischemic and ischemic. The ischemic form is defined by at least 10 disc areas of capillary non-perfusion on fluorescein angiography (posterior pole view). The CVOS (Central Retinal Vein Occlusion Study) found that prophylatic PRP for ischemic CRVO did *not* completely prevent the development of iris or angle neovascularization and that future PRP was less effective. Specifically, 20% with ischemic CRVO still developed iris/angle neovascularization. Therefore, PRP is only recommended when iris or angle neovascularization first occurs. The CVOS also found that macular grid laser did *not* significantly improve visual acuity in CVO patients with macular edema. However, there was a trend toward improved outcomes for younger (<65 years old) patients, with *non-ischemic CRVO*, who received macular grid laser. Therefore, many retinal specialists will consider macular grid laser for these younger, perfused patients. Editor's note: of course with the results of the BRAVO/CRUISE studies, use of anti-VEGF medications like ranibizumab is now the most popular way of treating macular edema associated with branch and central vein occlusions. explanation: This patient has a branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO). For macular edema caused by a BRVO, the BVOS (Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion Study) recommended waiting for 3 months to allow for spontaneous resolution of edema and blood. Eyes with macular edema are then treated with grid laser if visual acuity is 20/40 or worse. In addition, a fluorescein angiogram (FA) must demonstrate the absence of macular non-perfusion. If macular non-perfusion is present on FA, then laser should not be undertaken. In current practice, anti-VEGF agents are first line therapy for RVO-related macular edema [though intravitreal steroids such as triamcinolone or sustained release dexamethasone (Ozurdex) may be considered first line for pseudophakic patients]. More recent studies (BRAVO/CRUISE) have also shown that delaying treatment for even a few months (as was done in the BVOS) may lead to worse outcomes and so treatment for RVO-related macular edema is no longer delayed as in the BVOS. explanation: This patient presents with the typical "blood and thunder" fundus appearance of a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). This is demonstrated by the diffuse intraretinal hemorrhages, swollen optic nerve, and acutely-decreased vision. The CRUISE study1, published in 2010, investigated the effect of intravitreal ranibizumab (0.3 and 0.5 mg doses) versus sham injection on CRVO-associated macular edema involving the fovea. The treatment protocol consisted of monthly intravitreal ranibizumab injections for 6 months followed by a 6-month "observation period" during which all participants could receive additional injections according to a pre-specified reinjection protocol. This pivotal study showed that both ranibizumab dosages were highly effective in improving the vision of patients with CRVO-associated macular edema. Specifically, at the initial 6-month endpoint, the mean change from baseline visual acuity (the primary endpoint) was a gain of 12.7 and 14.9 letters in the ranibizumab groups compared to only 0.8 letters in the sham injection group. The drug groups also showed significant positive results for other visual parameters (e.g. gain of at least 15 letters) as well as quality-of-life scores. The same issue of Ophthalmology in which the CRUISE study was published also contained articles for the initial BRAVO2 and Ozurdex3 results. Briefly, the BRAVO trial was an analogous trial to CRUISE which enrolled patients with BRVO-associated macular edema. It showed similar results to the CRUISE trial. The Ozurdex trial (GENEVA) (Answer "B") showed the efficacy of a single dexamethasone intravitreal implant on macular edema associated with either BRVOs or CRVOs. explanation: The photograph demonstrates abnormally-dilated retinal vessels with abnormal arteriovenous communications. This finding is typical of retinal racemose angioma (aka congenital retinal arteriovenous malformation) which is a developmental malformation by which there is no intervening capillary bed between some retinal arteries and veins. These malformations are typically unilateral, non-hereditary, and can be associated with poor vision if the fovea is involved. In addition, these abnormal vessels are at risk for obstruction and subsequent neovascularization. Notably, these abnormal vessels do not leak on FA. Instead, there is rapid venous filling since there is no intervening capillary bed. This vascular malformation may be associated with the phakomatosis, Wyburn- Mason syndrome. The systemic manifestations of this syndrome include ipsilateral vascular malformations of the brain, orbit and mandible. The vascular abnormalities of the mandible may present with unexpected bleeding after a "routine" tooth extraction. In the case of visually-significant macular edema, the RAM may be lightly treated with photocoagulation using a larger spot size (e.g. 200 to 500 microns). explanation: Leber miliary aneurysms (i.e. unilateral parafoveal telangiectasia type 1) typically occurs in males and resembles a macular variant of Coats disease with a circinate type of exudates. When edema is present, laser photocoagulation may be indicated and can be successful in resolving exudation. Type 2 bilateral parafoveal telangiectasia has equal sex predilection and affects both eyes. Perifoveal (mostly temporal) retinal changes typically include thickening, loss of transparency with grayish appearance, small telangiectatic vessels, and a cystic appearance of the fovea. Choroidal neovascularization may develop. Approximately one-third of patients with this variant will have an abnormal glucose tolerance test. This condition does not typically respond to laser photocoagulation but may show some improvement with anti-VEGF agents. Patients with type 3 bilateral parafoveal telangiectasia with retinal capillary obliteration show vision loss from the loss of perifoveal capillaries. Type 3, like type 2, does not respond well to laser photocoagulation. Retinal macroaneurysms are acquired ectasias of mostly second-order retinal arterioles. Vision loss may occur from occlusion of the arteriole or due to hemorrhage. Hemorrhage may span all layers of the retina (e.g. vitreous hemorrhage, sub-ILM, intraretinal or subretinal). Retinal edema is also a cause of vision loss in these cases. The most common association with retinal arterial macroaneurysms is chronic hypertension (two-thirds of cases). Laser photocoagulation can be considered in cases of vision loss due to macular edema. Thrombosis and subsequent arterial obstruction is a possible complication of laser photocoagulation treatment of macroaneurysms. explanation: The patient has an acquired retinal macroaneurysm (RAM) located on the inferior arcade. RAM develop in the sixth to seventh decade of life, typically off of a third order arterial branch. The most common risk factor is hypertension. They are more common in women, and are more frequent in the right eye, but are bilateral in 10% of cases. Visual symptoms are typically due to exudation spreading into the macula. However, spontaneous bleeding may also occur (sometimes precipitated by Valsalva); are at multiple retinal levels (e.g., subretinal, under the internal limiting membrane, subhyaloid, and vitreous); and cause sudden vision loss. Pathology shows a break in the arterial wall closed off by a fibrin platelet clot and surrounded by varying amounts of blood, exudate, macrophages, hemosiderin, and a fibroglial reaction. Prognosis is excellent with many aneurysms spontaneously closing by thrombosis after a period of exudation or bleeding. Patients with chronic exudation or bleeding in the macula are at greatest risk of permanent vision loss. As spontaneous healing is frequent, treatment is not often indicated, but should be considered with persistent exudation within the fovea. Treatment is with laser photocoagulation with large- spot-size and long-duration focused at the aneurysm. WRONG ANSWERS: • Spontaneous rupture can cause acute loss of vision; however most bleeding RAMs have an excellent prognosis with spontaneous resolution. • Multiple lesions may develop due to focal arterial wall aging defects, but this is not an indication for treatment. • Hemorrhage may occur at multiple levels of the retina (e.g., subretinal, under the internal limiting membrane, subhyaloid, and vitreous). However, most bleeding RAMs have an excellent prognosis with spontaneous resolution. explanation: This fundus photograph shows multiple confluent soft drusen, many of which are more than 125 microns in size. This photograph is characteristic for a patient with "intermediate" (Category 3) age-related macular degeneration (AMD) as defined by the original AREDS trial. This patient would benefit from AREDS vitamin supplementation to reduce the chance of developing advanced AMD. The original AREDS vitamin formulation consisted of vitamin C, vitamin E, beta carotene, zinc oxide, and cupric oxide. Caution should be used in using beta-carotene in current or past smokers since there appears to be a higher risk of lung cancer for this sub-population of patients. The more recent AREDS2 formulation replaces the beta-carotene component with lutein and zeaxanthin. A post-hoc subgroup analysis done in AREDS2 compared lutein + zeaxanthin + AREDS without beta carotene versus the original AREDS formulation (i.e. had beta-carotene). This analysis found a hazard ratio of 0.82 in favor of the lutein + zeathanin + AREDS without beta carotene for progression to advanced AMD. Thus, the AREDS2 recommended that the beta-carotene component be completely replaced with lutein + zeathanin (in addition to the concern of increased lung cancer in former/current smokers). explanation: The VISION study was the first pivotal study demonstrating the efficacy of anti- VEGF agents in the treatment of neovascular age-related macular degeneration. In this study, patients were randomized to placebo or pegaptanib (i.e. Macugen) at doses of 0.3 mg, 1.0 mg, or 3.0 mg. At 1 year, 45% of patients receiving placebo suffered moderate vision loss (i.e. 3 lines or more) compared to 30%, 29%, and 35% in the 0.3 mg, 1.0 mg, and 3.0 mg pegaptanib groups. In addition, pegaptanib showed efficacy for all lesion types. Answer choice "A" refers to the MARINA (minimally classic/occult trial of the anti- VEGF antibody ranibizumab in the treatment of neovascular AMD) trial which randomized patients with minimally classic or occult lesions to placebo or monthly ranibizumab injections (0.3 mg and 0.5 mg doses) for 2 years. At 1 year, ~95% of both ranibizumab groups lost fewer than 15-letters as compared to 62.2% of patients receiving sham injections. Also, visual acuity improved by 15 or more letters in 24.8%, 33.8%, and 5.0% in the 0.3 mg, 0.5 mg, and placebo groups respectively. These benefits of ranibizumab were maintained at the 2-year endpoint. Answer choice "B" refers to the CATT (Comparison of AMD Treatments Trial). Basically at 1 year, bevacizumab (i.e. Avastin) was found equivalent to ranibizumab on both a monthly and as-needed basis. Answer choice "C" refers to the VIEW-1 and 2 studies which demonstrated the noninferiority of aflibercept (i.e. VEGF Trap-Eye) to monthly ranibizumab. Importantly, one study arm demonstrated that the regimen of aflibercept every 2 months (after 3 initial monthly doses) was equivalent to monthly ranibizumab. -------------------------- Q-Which of the following micronutrients was NOT used in the original AREDS (Age Related Eye Disease Study) trial but was studied in the AREDS2 trial and did NOT demonstrate a benefit in the prevention of advanced AMD (age-related macular degeneration)?

explanation: The original AREDS (Age-Related Eye Disease Study) used the following categories to define the stages of AMD and the patient's likelihood of developing "advanced" AMD: • Category 1 (No AMD) -- no or few small (<63 microns in diameter) drusen. This was the control group in the AREDS study. Actually, 0.45% of these patients progressed to advanced AMD. • Category 2 (Early AMD) -- extensive small drusen, pigment abnormalities, or at least 1 intermediate (63-124 microns) size druse. These patients had only a 1.3% probability of progression to advanced AMD by 5 years. • Category 3 (Intermediate AMD) -- extensive intermediate drusen; at least one large ( ≥125 microns) druse; or noncentral geographic atrophy (GA). These patients had a 18% probability of progression to advanced AMD by 5 years. • Category 4 (Advanced AMD) -- at least one of the following: o GA involving the foveal center o presence of CNV o serous or hemorrhagic detachment of the neurosensory retina or RPE o Retinal hard exudates o Subretinal and sub-RPE fibrovascular proliferation o Disciform scar o (Thus, if a patient had advanced AMD in one eye, then the AREDS found a 43% probability of progression to advanced AMD in the fellow eye at 5 years) Since these categories are somewhat difficult to remember, a simplified 4-point grading system was developed by AREDS to classify the severity of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) and to predict an individual's risk of developing advanced AMD in one eye. This grading system is as follows: • presence of any pigment abnormalities -- 1 point • presence of 1 or more large (≥125 micron in diameter) drusen -- 1 point • presence of neovascular AMD -- 2 points • for patients with no large drusen, presence of bilateral intermediate (63- 124 microns) drusen -- 1 point These risk factors are added over both eyes and have a range from 0 to 4. The 5- and 10-year risk of developing AMD in 1 eye is as follows: • 0 points: 0.5% risk over 5 years 1% risk over 10 years • 1 point: 3% risk over 5 years 7% risk over 10 years • 2 points: 12% risk over 5 years 22% risk over 10 years • 3 points 25% risk over 5 years 50% risk over 10 years • 4 points: 50% risk over 5 years 67% risk over 10 years Also, reticular pseudodrusen (aka subretinal drusenoid deposits) have been associated with a greater risk for choroidal neovascularization (CNV) and geographic atrophy (GA). The BCSC also specifically states that an eye with soft and confluent drusen is more likely to progress to CNV than one with only hard drusen. Answer "D" would be a patient with "AREDS Category 2" (or "Early") AMD and thus would have the least likelihood (~1.3% over 5 years) of progressing to advanced AMD. Clinical Pearl: to determine if a druse is "large" (i.e. ≥125 microns in diameter), compare its size to a vein width near the optic disc margin. Vein widths here are estimated to be ~120-150 microns in diameter. Q-Which of the following is considered a susceptibility gene for the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?

question: Which of the following is considered a susceptibility gene for the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?
explanation: The BCSC specifically mentions two specific susceptibility genes for the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD): • CFH (1q31) o This gene codes for complement factor H. o The CFH Y402H mutation confers a 4.6-fold increased risk for AMD when heterozygous and a 7.4-fold increased risk when homozygous. • ARMS2 (10q26) o "Age-Related Maculopathy Susceptibility 2" o Poorly understood gene product and function o ARMS2 A69S mutation confers a 2.7-fold increased risk for AMD when heterozygous and an 8.2-fold increased risk when homozyous. If an individual is homozygous for these mutations in both genes, the risk for AMD is an astonishing 50-fold higher. Mutations in CHM are responsible for choroideremia. This is an X-linked recessive disease which is characterized by widespread and progressive degeneration of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and choriocapillaris. Studies have localized the CHM gene product to the RPE. These individuals typically develop night blindness during the first or second decade of life, and later develop ring scotomata similar to retinitis pigmentosa. However, most patients with this disease maintain good central visual acuity for 4 or 5 decades. Mutations in VMD2 (BEST1; chromosome 11) are responsible for Best disease. These individuals typically have a yellow, "yolk-like" macular lesion present in childhood. This "yolk" eventually breaks down leaving a mottled geographic atrophy pattern. Individuals with Best disease have relatively-good (e.g. 20/30) vision despite the dramatic appearance of the macular lesions. This condition is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. Mutations in OAT are responsible for gyrate atrophy. This condition is characterized by geographic paving-stone-like areas of atrophy that coalesce to form a scalloped border between abnormal and normal RPE. Gyrate atrophy is an autosomal recessive condition. Mutations in OAT result in markedly-high elevations of ornithinewhich is toxic to the retina and choroid. Treatment consists of dietary arginine restriction (if possible) and vitamin B6 supplementation (if the patient is actually responsive to this therapy). Other findings in gyrate atrophy include: posterior subcapsular cataracts, and high myopia with high astigmatism. Visual acuity is usually normal in these patients until the age of 10 years. Q-Which of the following vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) isoforms is thought to be the most pathologic in neovascular AMD (age-related macular degeneration)?

question: Which of the following vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) isoforms is thought to be the most pathologic in neovascular AMD (age-related macular degeneration)?

Q-Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the different types of choroidal neovascularization (CNV)?

question: Which of the following statements is TRUE regarding the different types of choroidal neovascularization (CNV)?

options.D: Type 3 neovascularization originates in the capillary plexus of the retina and grown toward the RPE
options.C: Type 2 neovascularization typically appears as a area of red discoloration often associated with an exudate
options.B: Type 1 neovascularization occupies the compartment between the RPE and outer segments of the retina
options.A: Type 2 neovascularization is the most common form of CNV

explanation: The BCSC specifically indicates an anatomical classification for choroidal neovascularization: • Type 1 CNV o Occurs when new vessels from the choriocapillaris grow through a defect in the Bruch membrane into the sub-RPE space. o Leakage and bleeding can lead to the vascularized serous or fibrovascular pigment epithelial detachment (PED). These fibrovascular PEDs often have an irregular contour. o Previously, known as "occult" CNV. o Poorly-delineated and stains late with irregular margins during fluorescein angiography. • Type 2 CNV o When abnormal vessels from the choriocapillaris penetrate through the RPE. Thus, type 2 CNV is located between the RPE and the outer segments of the retina. o Less common than type 1 CNV. o Has a lacy or gray-green appearance on fundus exam. o Previously, known as "classic" CNV. o Has a well-demarcated vascular pattern early on fluorescein angiography. The fluorescein dye then pools into the subneurosensory retinal space. • Type 3 CNV o Originates from blood vessels sprouting from the deep capillary plexus of the retina which grow downward toward the RPE. o Were originally called retinal angiomatous proliferations. o Appear as a small area of red discoloration frequently associated with an exudate. Q-A 55-year old woman presented with an asymptomatic fundus lesion identified incidentally after cataract surgery in the left eye. Which of the following conditions is most likely?

question: A 55-year old woman presented with an asymptomatic fundus lesion identified incidentally after cataract surgery in the left eye. Which of the following conditions is most likely?
explanation: Peripheral exudative hemorrhagic chorioretinopathy (PEHCR) is a peripheral (usually temporal) choroidal neovascular membrane (CNVM). This entity is typically seen in the periphery of an older (mean: 77 years old) woman (69%) and is often asymptomatic. Approximately 25% of patients experience bilateral lesions. Treatment with anti-VEGF injections are sometimes recommended if exudation encroaches the macula. However, these lesions can often be observed as they are not sight-threatening in the same way as macular CNVMs. WRONG ANSWERS: • Choroidal melanoma would be the next most likely of the answer choices, but the presence of hard exudates on the edge closest to the macula makes this less likely, as melanomas rarely exude lipid. • Rhegmatogenous retinal detachments almost always cause symptoms of floaters or flashing lights. • Acute retinal necrosis typically presents with floaters, reduced vision, and pain. Q-Which of the following is NOT considered to be a risk factor for the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?

question: Which of the following is NOT considered to be a risk factor for the development of age-related macular degeneration (AMD)?
explanation: Most population-based studies have found that the most important factor in developing age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is advanced age. In resource-rich countries, approximately 10% of individuals over the age of 65 years and 25% over the age of 75 years have AMD. Other classic risk factors: • Female • Cigarette smoking • Hypertension • Hypercholesterolemia • Positive family history • Cardiovascular disease • Light iris color • Caucasian race • Hyperopia The BCSC specifically mentions the MESA (Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis) study which found the prevalence of AMD to be highest in whites and lowest in African Americans. question: A patient with no significant past ocular history aside from cataract undergoes cataract surgery complicated by vitreous loss. Based on the history and OCT findings, what is the most likely pathophysiology of this finding?

options.D: Retinal ischemia induced release of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)

explanation: The OCT demonstrates prominent cystoid macular edema (CME). CME after cataract surgery is also known as Irvine-Gass syndrome. There are many causes for CME including vitreomacular traction, inflammation / uveitis, diabetes, X-linked hereditary retinoschisis, epiretinal membrane, and retinitis pigmentosa. Following cataract surgery the most important influences are inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins that disrupt blood vessel integrity resulting in leakage of fluid into the macula. Vitreomacular traction (VMT) can occur following vitreous loss during cataract surgery and can cause CME, but there is no evidence of VMT on this OCT. The first treatment for most cases of CME (including post-surgical CME) is medical therapy with topical steroids and topical NSAIDs. Q-Which of the following is generally FALSE regarding polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV)?

question: Which of the following is generally FALSE regarding polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV)?

options.D: fluorescein angiography (FA) is the optimal method of diagnosing PCV
options.C: The most frequent presentations of PCV are serous or hemorrhagic detachments of the retina and RPE
options.B: PCV lesions have a predilection to being located in the peripapillary region
options.A: PCV is classically described to occur in hypertensive middle-aged women of African or Asian ancestry

explanation: PCV was originally described by Yannuzzi et al in 1982 as a distinct form of choroidal neovascularization with a predilection for the peripapillary area. It is characterized by dilated choroidal vascular channels terminating in "polyps" leading to serous and hemorrhagic detachments of the retina and RPE. Another key feature is that there is either minimal or no cystic change of the overlying retina even if the subretinal hemorrhage is severe. Unlike choroidal neovascularization solely associated with age-related macular degeneration (AMD), PCV is classically associated with more darkly-pigmented individuals (e.g. Blacks and Asians). In fact, some experts believe that virtually all African American patients with neovascular AMD have concomitant PCV. In some clinical studies from Japan, over 50% of neovascular AMD patients had PCV. Also in contrast to neovascular AMD, PCV is not typically associated with drusen. Q-Though FA is routinely used in the evaluation of choroidal neovascularization in general, ICG angiography is much more helpful in the diagnosis and management of PCV. This is because the longer wavelengths used in ICG are able to penetrate more deeply into the choroid and also past any thick hemorrhage. What is the primary goal in using a preferential hyperacuity perimeter (PHP) for a patient?

question: What is the primary goal in using a preferential hyperacuity perimeter (PHP) for a patient?

options.D: to estimate visual acuity in non-verbal children
options.C: to detect higher order aberrations in preparation for refractive surgery
options.A: to detect early paracentral glaucomatous visual field defects

explanation: The PHP is a visual field analyzer used specifically to detect new-onset neovascular AMD and to distinguish it from non-neovascular AMD. It is more sensitive than Amsler grid screening in detecting visual changes related to neovascular AMD. It uses the "Vernier acuity phenomenon" which is based on our ability to perceive a small difference in the spatial localization of two or more stimuli. This property permits the detection of early metamorphopsia caused by the displacement of photoreceptors by a choroidal neovascular membrane. Q-A 61-year-old female presents with the complaint of gradually reducing vision in the right eye for 6 months. She denies having any medical problems and does not take any medications. She has never had any eye surgeries, and until 6 months ago, was seeing "20/20." On examination, her best-corrected visual acuity is 20/60 OD. The images depict her condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management option?

question: The images depict her condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management option?

options.D: Pars Plana Vitrectomy with membrane peeling OD

explanation: The images depict an epiretinal membrane (ERM) with secondary cystoid macular edema (CME). Notice the prominent retinal striae on the color fundus photograph. A) Observation is inappropriate given that the patient is symptomatic and has moderately reduced vision. Since she has noticed worsening vision over the past 6 months, the vision is likely to continue deteriorating if observation is continued. B) Anti-VEGF therapy is inappropriate given that it has no efficacy for this condition. The CME is due to the circumfrential tractional forces exerted by the ERM on the retinal blood vessels running through the nerve fiber layer, and is not caused by inflammatory mediators. C) Topical or intravitreal steroids are inappropriate for this condition for the same reason as described for anti-VEGF therapy. D) Pars plana vitrectomy with membrane peeling +/- internal limiting peeling is the appropriate option. Once the ERM is removed and the tractional forces are relieved, the CME resolves. Removing the internal limiting membrane along with the ERM will prevent recurrence of the ERM. An ERM is unable re-proliferate on the surface of the nerve fiber layer, which in part explains the popularity of internal limiting membrane peeling by vitreoretinal surgeons. question: A 75-year-old male smoker presents with six months of night and peripheral vision loss. His OCT image as shown below is similar in both eyes. Which of the following would help to support the putative diagnosis?

options.C: Anterior chamber paracentesis for viral DNA

explanation: The key finding in this OCT image is attenuation of the parafoveal ellipsoid zone (IS/OS) boundary. This is representative of a photoreceptor degeneration and can occur in inherited retinal dystrophies such as retinitis pigmentosa or cone dystrophy. The demographic information suggests a recent rapid progression in an older male, so consideration needs to be given for cancer- associated retinopathy (CAR). The modality most useful to help identify generalized retinal dysfunction is the electroretinogram (ERG). WRONG ANSWERS: • RNFL OCT can help identify optic disc pallor, but this can also be seen in glaucoma or inherited retinal dystrophies. • Anterior chamber paracentesis for viral DNA would be useful for ruling out viral- mediated anterior uveitis, cytomegalovirus retinitis, acute retinal necrosis, or progressive outer retinal necrosis. • B-scan ultrasound would be most useful in this case if there was concern of an exudative retinal detachment or scleritis, but these are not described in the question. Q-A 30-year old lawyer presents to your office with new-onset metamorphopsia in the right eye. Dilated fundus exam and fluorescein angiogram (FA) are seen above. Which of the following FA patterns is most common in this condition?

question: Which of the following FA patterns is most common in this condition?
explanation: Central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) is characterized by the development of well-delineated serous retinal or RPE detachments. It typically occurs in young men and has some association with type A personalities and periods of high stress (although this relationship has never been proven). The most common FA pattern is the "expansile dot" pattern; the least common pattern is the "diffuse pattern." Although some residents think the "smokestack" pattern occurs commonly in CSCR, it actually only occurs in approximately 10% of cases. Q-A 53-year-old man presents with decreased vision in the right eye for the past several months. OCT of the right eye is shown above. Which of the following is TRUE regarding this disease process?

question: A 53-year-old man presents with decreased vision in the right eye for the past several months. OCT of the right eye is shown above. Which of the following is TRUE regarding this disease process?

options.D: Intravitreal injection of ocriplasmin has been shown to resolve this problem in approximately one-quarter of patients
options.C: Hyalocytes are the predominant cell type involved in this disease process
options.B: Surgical correction typically results in vision improvement in about 33% of eyes
options.A: The patient most likely has a Mittendorf dot accompanying this lesion

explanation: The OCT clearly demonstrates the process of vitreomacular traction (VMT) with tenting-up of the retina due to incomplete separation of the posterior vitreous at the macula. This traction can also result in cystic edema and a shallow retinal detachment. Typical clinical symptoms include decreased and distorted vision. On exam, there is often an abnormal vitreous opacity overlying the macular region with traction on the macula and also the optic nerve. Because of this traction, fluorescein angiogram may show leakage of dye from the macular retinal vessels and from the optic disc. VMT is a subset of epiretinal membrane and glial cells are the predominant cell type involved. Surgical correction of VMT has been demonstrated to result in visual improvement of two lines or greater in 75% of eyes.1 Ocriplasmin2 is a recombinant protease that targets fibronectin and laminin. Ocriplasmin is administered through an intravitreal injection. By causing separation at the vitreoretinal interface, some patients can avoid surgery. At day 28, 26% of ocriplasmin injected eyes had resolution of vitreomacular adhesion vs. 10% of placebo-injected eyes. question: A 60-year-old patient presents with a recent decline in vision, 8 weeks after cataract surgery. The patient's OCT is presented here. Which of the following would be an INAPPROPRIATE treatment for the ocular condition shown in the spectral domain OCT above?

options.C: Vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peeling

explanation: The OCT demonstrates prominent cystoid macular edema (CME). There are many causes for CME including post-surgical (e.g., Irvine-Gass syndrome), vitreomacular traction (VMT), inflammation / uveitis, diabetes, X-linked hereditary retinoschisis, epiretinal membrane, and retinitis pigmentosa. The most important influence on CME formation is inflammatory mediators such as prostaglandins that disrupt blood vessel integrity resulting in leakage of fluid into the macula. For this reason, the first treatment for most cases of CME (including post-surgical CME) is medical therapy with topical steroids and topical NSAIDs. With severe CME or CME refractory to topical treatment, subtenon's kenalog is often utilized. Vitrectomy with internal limiting membrane peel would only be appropriate if the patient demonstrated traction on the macula from an epiretinal membrane or VMT. If present, such traction would be visible on a high quality spectral domain OCT such as this figure. Remember that one goal of standardized tests is to identify inappropriate risk taking. Always think twice before choosing a surgical intervention as an answer choice when an effective medical intervention is also an option. • • Q-A 23-year-old female with no past ocular or medical history presents with 3 weeks of central visual loss and flashing lights in her left eye. question: A 23-year-old female with no past ocular or medical history presents with 3 weeks of central visual loss and flashing lights in her left eye. She demonstrates 20/60 vision in the left eye and a mild left afferent pupillary defect. Her fundus examination is remarkable only for retinal pigment epithelium stippling in the left eye and mild disc edema. The right eye vision and exam is normal. An OCT and FA is performed and results from the left eye are shown above. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is a poorly understood, idiopathic inflammatory condition of the inner choroid and/or outer retina. It tends to occur unilaterally in younger myopic females and often presents with central vision loss, enlarged blind spot, and photopsias. Photopsias are very characteristic of MEWDS and other poorly understood inflammatory conditions such as acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) and idiopathic enlarged blind spot syndrome; photopsias as a prominent feature in a young patient with central vision loss should raise suspicion for these conditions. The hallmark features of MEWDS are short-lived white dots usually lasting from days to a week after visual symptoms begin, macular pigment stippling, macular wreath- like punctuate hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography, and mild disc edema in some cases. With the advent of high quality spectral domain OCT (SD-OCT) images, it has been discovered that there are non-specific but characteristic outer segment and RPE changes on SD-OCT. Essentially the OCT shows disruption of the usual contour of these layers without evidence of retinal edema. Similar changes can be seen in AZOOR, commotio retinae, and solar retinopathy. In the correct clinical context, however, the disruption of the normal inner segment- outer segment and RPE layers is essentially diagnostic of MEWDS. This is helpful in cases such as this question where the white dots have long since resolved by the time the patient is examined. explanation: Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is a poorly understood, idiopathic inflammatory condition of the inner choroid and/or outer retina. It tends to occur unilaterally in younger myopic females and often presents with central vision loss, enlarged blind spot, and photopsias. Other causes of photopsias associated with vision loss are often short lasting (migraine), have prominent exam findings (retinal detachment or tears), or don't typically present in a young patient (cancer-associated retinopathy and melanoma- associated retinopathy). The hallmark features of MEWDS are short-lived white dots usually lasting from days to a week after visual symptoms begin, macular pigment stippling, macular wreath-like punctuate hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography, and mild disc edema in some cases. Recently with the advent of high quality spectral domain OCT (SD-OCT) images, it has been discovered that there are non-specific but characteristic outer segment and RPE changes on SD-OCT. Essentially the OCT shows disruption of the usual contour of these layers without evidence of retinal edema. Similar changes can be seen in AZOOR, commotio retinae, and solar retinopathy. In the correct clinical context, however, the disruption of the normal ellipsoid zone and RPE layers is essentially diagnostic of MEWDS. question: A 64-year-old Caucasian male is referred to your clinic for a 1-month history of blurry vision in his left eye. He denies any recent ocular or head trauma, and his ocular history includes trace nuclear sclerotic cataracts in both eyes. On exam, his best corrected visual acuity in the left eye measures 20/100 and does not improve with pinhole. Posterior examination does not show a posterior vitreous detachment, and retinal findings correlate with optical coherence tomography imaging shown above. What in-office test can be performed to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation: As you may have guessed, all of the answers are eponymous tests from famous ophthalmologists. The patient’s symptoms and imaging data all indicate that he has a macular hole, specifically stage 3. The macular hole staging nomenclature adheres to the following parameters: • Stage 1 – also known as an impending macular hole, it demonstrates a loss of foveal depression without full thickness break. • Stage 2 – full thickness break ≤ 400 microns in diameter with the posterior hyaloid still attached to the fovea on OCT imaging. • Stage 3 – full thickness break > 400 microns with the posterior hyaloid noted to be detached over the macula; however, vitreous is still attached to the optic nerve head (thus, no posterior vitreous detachment observed on exam such as in our patient). • Stage 4 – same as stage 3 with the addition of a complete PVD. A full thickness macular hole can be difficult to discern from a partial thickness lamellar hole on fundus examination. If you do not have the luxury of OCT imaging, you can perform a Watze- Allen test (choice A) at the slit lamp. Using a 78D or 90D noncontact lens, a thin beam of light is projected over the macula across the fovea, and the patient is asked to report on its appearance. If the patient notices a break in the line, this may indicate a full thickness macular hole. The Jones test (choice B) is used to evaluate the lacrimal drainage system and is composed of two separate tests. The Jones I test investigates lacrimal outflow under normal physiologic conditions. The examiner places fluorescein into the conjunctival fornices and recovers it in the inferior nasal meatus by passing a cotton-tipped wire applicator into the region of the ostium of the nasolacrimal duct at 2 and 5 minutes. The Jones II test involves flushing residual fluorescein from the conjunctival sac using normal saline following an unsuccessful Jones I test to determine whether any reflux upon irrigation contains fluorescein in the retrieved fluid. There is no such thing as a Krimsky-Hirschberg test (choice C); however, there are separate Krimsky and Hirschberg tests. Both are used as screening tests to evaluate for the presence of strabismus. The Hirschberg test is performed by shining a light on the person’s eyes and observing where the light reflects off the corneas. In a person who is orthophoric, the light reflex lies slightly nasal from the center as a result of the cornea acting as a temporally-turned convex mirror to the observer. The light reflexes of both eyes are compared and should be symmetrical. Exotropia would demonstrate the corneal light reflex more nasally, and esotropia would show it more temporally. Similarily, hypertropia would demonstrate the reflex more inferiorly, and hypotropia would demonstrate it more superiorly. The Krimsky test employs the same principles as the Hirschberg test with the addition of prisms to quantify the amount of deviation by determining how much prism is required to re-center the reflex. The Marcus-Gunn test is typically how one checks for the presence of a relative afferent pupillary defect (rAPD) in clinic. It is performed by shining a light into the left and right eyes rapidly and comparing pupillary constriction. A normal response would be equal constriction of both pupils regardless of which eye the light is directed at, indicating an intact direct and consensual pupillary light reflex. When the test is performed in an eye with a rAPD, light directed in the affected eye will cause only mild constriction of both pupils, while light in the unaffected eye will cause a normal constriction of both pupils. The key is to remember that rAPD is “relative”, thus if there is pathology affecting both pupillary light reflexes, then this test is no longer valid. question: A 44-year-old-woman presents with decreased central vision. Her review of systems is notable for the presence of the skin finding seen in the external photo on the far left. Which of the following fundus photos is associated with this woman's condition?
explanation: The external photograph depicts the yellowish papular lesions that are synonymous with pseudoxanthoma elasticuma (PXE). This skin change resembles "chicken skin" and mainly affects the neck (as in this case), armpits, groin, and flexural creases. The main ocular findings associated with PXE are a "peau d'orange" fundus and angioid streaks (photo C). Other ocular findings in PXE include optic disc drusen and round atrophic scars. Vision loss from angioid streaks can occur from either submacular hemorrhages or choroidal neovascular membranes. These eyes are at higher risk of choroidal rupture after even mild ocular trauma. Photo "A" is depicting serpiginous choroidopathy; photo "B" is showing ocular histoplasmosis; and photo "D" is demonstrating multiple evascent white dot syndrome. explanation: Förster-Fuchs (i.e. not Dalen-Fuchs) spots can be found in pathologic myopia. These are dark spots due to RPE hyperplasia that presumably occur in response to a small choroidal neovascular lesion that does not progress. According to the BCSC, individuals with pathologic myopia have a spherical equivalent greater than -8.00 D and/or an axial length greater than 32.5 mm. Other findings found in pathologic myopia include: • optic disc tilting with extensive peripapillary atrophy • lacquer cracks • posterior staphyloma • atrophy of the RPE and choroid • elongation/atrophy of the ciliary body • lattice, cystoid, paving-stone degeneration • choroidal neovascularization • peripheral retinal holes. Dalen-Fuchs *nodules* occur in sympathetic ophthalmia and VKH syndrome. Q-A 39-year-old woman presents with acute metamorphopsia in the left eye. options.B: geographic atrophy from age-related macular degeneration (AMD)

explanation: The photo shows a hypopigmented, round excavated defect of the temporal optic disc consistent with an optic pit. Optic pits most commonly occur in the inferotemporal portion of the optic disc and may lead to serous macular detachments. There is some thought that the fluid contained within these serous detachments is either liquid vitreous or cerebrospinal fluid. The most common visual field defect associated with an optic pit is either a paracentral or arcuate scotoma. Of the answer choices above, CSCR is the one that is commonly associated with serous macular detachments due to a RPE defect. Q-A 63-year-old male presents for evaluation of the left eye following pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) for an epiretinal membrane (ERM). Two weeks ago, the patient underwent PPV with membrane peeling and internal limiting membrane (ILM) peeling. The patient's preoperative best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OS. The patient's best-corrected visual acuity is now 20/60 OS. The image depicts the patient's condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option at this time?

question: The patient's preoperative best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OS. The patient's best-corrected visual acuity is now 20/60 OS. The image depicts the patient's condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option at this time?

options.C: PPV with further ILM peeling and intraocular gas tamponade with face down positioning for 7 days
options.B: PPV with intraocular gas tamponade and face down positioning for 3 days

explanation: The images depict an eccentric full-thickness macular hole (FTMH) following PPV with ERM removal and ILM peeling. These holes occur in approximately 2% of cases following ERM removal. Putative mechanisms for hole formation include weakening of the glial structure of the retina induced by the decapitation of Müller cells, opening or de-roofing of intraretinal cysts, contraction of residual ILM, direct mechanical trauma, and ILM-staining dye toxicity. A) Observation is the most appropriate choice. An eccentric FTMH has minimal impact on the patient's subjective visual function unless it occurs either close to the fovea (within one disc diameter) or in the nasal macula within the papillomacular bundle. Furthermore, an eccentric FTMH does not seem to readily accumulate subretinal fluid with subsequent retinal detachment, though there may be a small risk of retinal detachment in highly myopic patients. The hole in this case is in the temporal macula and more than one disc diameter away from the fovea. The level of visual acuity is appropriate for a patient 2 weeks after ERM removal. B/C) It is inappropriate to subject this patient to an additional surgical procedure given that the FTMH will likely remain stable and asymptomatic indefinitely. It is evident from the images that both the ERM and ILM have been sufficiently removed from the central macula. D) Intravitreal ocriplasmin is inappropriate given that the posterior hyaloid has already been completely removed during the ERM removal (as evidenced by the images). explanation: Angioid streaks are breaks or irregularities in Bruch's membrane which can lead to: (1) spontaneous subretinal hemorrhages that are *not* necessarily related to choroidal neovascularization (CNV). question: A 57-year-old Caucasian man presents to your clinic complaining of a gradual increase in metamorphopsia of his right eye vision for the past 6 months. His ocular history includes moderate myopia in both eyes corrected with eyeglasses. explanation: Based on the patient’s symptoms as well as imaging data, he has an epiretinal membrane (also known as macular pucker or cellophane maculopathy) of the right eye. The most common concurrent ocular finding in this condition is a posterior vitreous detachment (PVD), as this is present in approximately 60-90% of patients at the time of diagnosis. As the vitreous ages and pulls away from the macula, the retina can be subject to mild injury which induces a reactive gliosis from immune cells that generate the characteristic membranous tractional appearance. Progressive metamorphopsia and central vision loss are the most common presenting symptoms. Surgical intervention may be necessary depending upon the level of visual debilitation experienced by the patient. Image below is of a Weiss ring, which is a common clinical finding of a PVD. Pseudoexfoliation of the lens capsule is most commonly seen in patients with pseudoexfoliation syndrome, which often can lead to secondary glaucoma. Common findings include glaucomatous changes of the optic nerve head, fibrillary white flaky material on the lens capsule, and increased pigmentary deposition on the trabecular meshwork. Hollenhorst plaque is a cholesterol embolus often found within the lumen of the retinal artery that can cause a retinal artery occlusion (RAO). This can occur in the central retinal artery (CRAO) or one of its branches (BRAO). Hollenhorst plaques tend to originate from the carotid arteries or the aorta due to atherosclerotic lesions, and can lead to RAO when the plaque completely obstructs the vessel. Its presence is a confirming diagnosis; however, the absence of a plaque does not rule out the possibility of an embolic occlusion. The fundus will display typical ischemic findings such as retinal whitening around the occluded vessel, and the patient will experience painless vision loss. Retinal capillary hemangioma (also known as retinal hemangioblastoma) is a benign hamartoma (excess proliferation of normal tissue in a normal location) that is composed of tortuous, large-diameter capillaries in a nodular appearance with engorged feeding and draining blood vessels. It may exist by itself or as part of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, an autosomal dominantly inherited condition characterized by the development of capillary hemangiomas of the brain and spinal cord, renal cell carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, and other visceral cystic findings. • You examine a patient who complains of a persistent "blind spot" in both eyes after attending an "astronomical event" celebration. This commonly occurs in "sun gazers" or those viewing a solar eclipse. Many people mistakenly assume that directly viewing a solar eclipse is safe since it is perceived as being dimmer. Factors that are thought to be protective against this condition include: darker fundus pigmentation and high refractive errors. Factors that are thought to increase the risk of this condition are: being younger, having clearer crystalline lenses, and taking photosensitizing medications (e.g. tetracycline and psoralens). The initial (acute) fundus finding in solar retinopathy is this yellow-white dot which represents retinal edema. Oftentimes however, no fundus findings are seen acutely. After a few days, this becomes a reddish dot and then may evolve into a lamellar hole or depression. Besides topical steroids and NSAIDs, YAG vitreolysis of this strand will best resolve the CME. This is a non-invasive and relatively straightforward procedure. Here are some suggested steps/advice in performing this procedure: 1. Constrict the patient's pupil with pilocarpine (e.g. 1 or 2%). This will help with visualization of the culprit vitreous strands by placing them on tension. 2. Use a peripheral iridotomy lens. This will provide adequate magnification of the vitreous strands. 3. explanation: Polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV) was originally described by Yannuzzi et al in 1982 as a distinct form of choroidal neovascularization with a predilection for the peripapillary area. explanation: The GENEVA study was a multicenter, randomized clinical trial of 1267 participants that evaluated the efficacy and safety of the dexamethasone intravitreal implant (OZURDEX) compared with sham injections in eyes with vision loss due to macular edema associated with either a branch retinal vein occlusion (BRVO) or a central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO). At 6-months follow-up, the percentage of eyes with a > or =15-letter improvement in visual acuity was significantly higher in the dexamethasone intravitreal implant group compared with sham. The percentage of eyes with a > or =15-letter loss in visual acuity was significantly lower in the dexamethasone intravitreal implant group compared with sham at all follow-up visits. The percentage of dexamethasone intravitreal implant group-treated eyes with intraocular pressure of > or =25 mmHg peaked at 16% at day 60 and was not different from sham by day 180. There was no significant between-group difference in the occurrence of cataract or cataract surgery at 6-months follow-up. The researchers concluded that dexamethasone intravitreal implants can both reduce the risk of vision loss and improve the speed and incidence of visual improvement in eyes with macular edema secondary to BRVO or CRVO. This study established OZURDEX as a safe and effective treatment for macular edema secondary to a BRVO or CRVO. It typically occurs in males and the edema often responds to laser photocoagulation. Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO)-related macular edema is treated with anti- VEGF agents or intravitreal steroids (triamcinolone or dexamethasone intravitreal implant). Macular laser for CRVO-related edema was studied in the CVOS. Treatment with macular grid laser did decrease angiographic evidence of macular edema; howerver, it did not improve visual acuity. There was a trend toward better vision in younger individuals, but currently macular laser is not indicated for CRVO-related macular edema, Type 2 bilateral parafoveal telangiectasia typically does not respond to photocoagulation as leaky vessels are not the predominent feature. Anti-VEGF agents have shown some promise. Enhanced S-cone syndrome patients may develop what appears to be macular edema on OCT but more truly represents macular schisis. explanation: This vignette is alluding to the condition of ocular toxocariasis, which is a zoonotic infection caused by either Toxocara canis or Toxocara cati. Dogs and cats are the definitive hosts of these roundworms. These animals pass Toxocara eggs via their feces into the environment which are then ingested by humans (i.e. fecal-oral route of transmission). Common associations of transmission to humans include: sandboxes, playgrounds, kittens/puppies, pica eating disorder, and rarely undercooked meat. In humans, these organisms grow as larvae in the small intestine and then spread hematogenously via the portal circulation to various organs (e.g. eye, liver, heart, brain, muscle). Ocular toxocariasis is typically unilateral and presents most commonly via 1 of 3 presentations: • Peripheral granuloma o This can be associated with a fibrous brand that extends from the granuloma to a posterior location (e.g. optic disc or macula). • Posterior pole granuloma o This can lead to severe vision loss if the central macula is involved. • Panuveitis (moderate/severe) o This can mimic endogenous endophthalmitis. Any of these 3 common presentations can cause leukoria; thus ocular toxocariasis is in the differential diagnosis of retinoblastoma. One way of distinguishing ocular toxocariasis from retinoblastoma is the lack of calcium in the former condition. Since the ocular morbidity associated with this condition is thought to be due to the immune response against dead/dying larvae, systemic antihelminthic therapy is generally ineffective. Instead, local and systemic corticosteroids are the mainstays of treatment to reduce inflammation and its subsequent complications (e.g. macular edema). Systemic antihelminthic therapy (e.g. oral albendazole) may be considered if the larvae appear to be active, but steroids are still the mainstay of treatment. Oral albendazole is used in the treatment of visceral toxocariasis (fever, coughing, hepatomegaly, pneumonia, encephalitis) which rarely ever occurs simultaneously with ocular toxocariasis. Ocular toxocariasis is considered a clinical diagnosis; however, supportive laboratory tests that can be helpful include: antibody testing of ocular fluids or serums and/or recovering the actual larvae from vitrectomy specimens. Since the Toxocara ova are not shed in the human gastrointestinal tract, stool analysis has no role in the diagnosis. Q-A 45-year-old farmer injures his right eye while working in the fields. explanation: The photo above demonstrates a classic or fulminant presentation of cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. In the classic form of CMV retinitis, there are large areas of hemorrhage against a background of whitened, necrotic retina, typically along the vascular arcades in the distribution of the nerve fiber layer. HIV positive patients are at risk for CMV retinitis when the CD4 count is below 50 cells/µL (answer A). HIV positive patients with CMV retinitis should be treated with antiretroviral therapy as well as specific treatment for CMV. Treatment begins with high-dose induction therapy with a bridge to low-dose maintenance therapy. Options for high-dose induction therapy include the following: • Intravenous ganciclovir 5 mg/kg twice daily for 2 weeks • Intravenous foscarnet 90 mg/kg twice daily for 2 weeks • Oral valganciclovir 900 mg twice daily for 3 weeks For patients with vision-threatening, posteriorly-located CMV retinitis, induction therapy is often supplemented with intravitreal injection of ganciclovir or foscarnet. Following completion of induction therapy, patients should be maintained on low-dose maintenance therapy with either intravenous ganciclovir or foscarnet, or oral valganciclovir 900 mg daily. Typically, oral valganciclovir is preferred due to ease of administration unless the patient develops specific complications related to treatment (e.g. bone marrow suppression). Low-dose maintenance treatment should be continued until the CD4 count is sustained above 200 cells/µL (Answer C). Provided the retinitis has responded to treatment and the patient is maintained on antiretroviral therapy, anti-CMV medications may be safely discontinued at that time. explanation: The fundus photo depicts the classic findings of toxoplasmosis chorioretinitis: a focal area of inflammation adjacent to an old chorioretinal scar with overlying vitreous condensation. Soheilian et al1 demonstrated the efficacy of intravitreal clindamycin + dexamethasone for this disease. This article demonstrated comparable therapeutic effect compared to the classic "triple therapy" of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, folinic acid, and (later) prednisone use. One significant advantage of intravitreal injection, as compared to oral therapy, is the elimination of noncompliance as a cause of treatment failure. Another advantage of this intravitreal regimen is the reduction of systemic side effects (e.g. myelosuppression when using pyrimethamine). 1Soheilian M et al. Randomized trial of intravitreal clindamycin and dexamethasone versus pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and prednisolone in treatment of ocular toxoplasmosis. Ophthalmology. 2011;118:134-41. You suspect a patient to have post-traumatic endophthalmitis caused by Bacillus cereus. The patient states that he is severely allergic to vancomycin. Which of the following agents should be given intravitreally?

question: You suspect a patient to have post-traumatic endophthalmitis caused by Bacillus cereus. The patient states that he is severely allergic to vancomycin. Which of the following agents should be given intravitreally?
explanation: Endophthalmitis complicates approximately 2-7% of penetrating eye injuries. This incidence is increased in the setting of intraocular foreign bodies and in rural settings. Bacillus cereus is a catalase-positive, spore-forming gram positive bacillus bacteria. It rarely causes endophthalmitis overall (e.g. after cataract surgery), but accounts for ~25% of posttraumatic endophthalmitis especially in soil-contaminated wounds. Bacillus cereus associated endophthalmitis is very fulminant with a rapid and severe course often leading to loss of the eye. The most common intravitreal antibiotics used for Bacillus cereus endophthalmitis are vancomycin (preferred if possible) and clindamycin. B. cereus is typically resistant to pencillins and cephalosporins. One should avoid intravireal aminoglycoside antibiotics (e.g. gentamicin) due to the possible risk of retinal infarction. As an aside, intravitreal clindamycin (with or without dexamethasone) is also used as treatment for ocular toxoplasmosis (i.e. as an alternative to the "classic" treatment of sulfadiazine with pyrimethamine and prednisone). question: You look ultra carefully with your super 66 ultra deluxe lens and think you have found the culprit. Which of the following is a known North American reservoir for a pathogen that can cause this disease?
explanation: The photograph shows peripheral bone spicule hyperpigmentation. Bone spicules result from dispersion of pigment in the retinal pigment epithelial layer which leads to the formation of clumps that look similar to the microscopic appearance of bone formation. Bone spicules are classically present in retinitis pigmentosa, but can occur in many other diseases causing diffuse destruction of the RPE (e.g., old trauma, diffuse unilateral subacute neuroretinitis (DUSN), syphilis, etc). Unilateral retinitis pigmentosa is an exceedingly rare diagnosis and should always raise concerns for other diagnoses. The history in this patient is rather typical for DUSN and the question stem suggests that the examiner found the worm on fundus examination (which is the only way to conclusively make the diagnosis). DUSN usually occurs in otherwise healthy, young patients and is due to subretinal spread of a nematode resulting in decreased vision, uveitis (most often vitritis), optic disc edema, and choroidal / deep retinal hypopigmented lesions. The bone spicule formation is actually a sign of chronicity as the RPE reorganizes itself following injury and is not usually present in the early stages of the disease. DUSN has been associated with numerous different worms worldwide. In the USA there are two worms most commonly implicated. In the Southeast US and extending south into the Caribbean and Latin Amercia, a 400-700 µm canine roundworm by the name of Ancylostoma canium causes DUSN. In the Midwest the causative worm, Baylisascaris procyonis, is larger (1000-2000 µm) and predominately resides in raccoons when not destroying retinas. If the worm is found on examination and is not located beneath the fovea then the treatment is death by photocoagulation (laser). White footed mice are a reservoir for Lyme disease. Cats harbor toxoplasmosis. Pigs harbor the tapeworm taenia solium responsible for cysticercosis in humans. • A 27-year old woman presents to your office for a mild decrease in vision in the left eye. This retinal finding in conjunction with the history, is most commonly found in cat-scratch disease which presents in individuals exposed to cat saliva (not necessarily scratched by them). The systemic symptoms of this disease include fever, malaise, and lymphadenopathy. Parinaud oculoglandular syndrome occurs in ~7-10% of individuals with cat-scratch disease. question: • A 19-year-old male comes in with two weeks of decreased vision in the left eye that developed acutely over several days. His review of systems is otherwise normal including a lack of eye pain. On history and exam his right eye is normal. In his left eye he has 20/200 best corrected vision, a 1+ left afferent pupillary defect, and diminished color plates. A Humphrey visual field (30-2) shows global depression in the left eye. The fundus exam of the left eye is shown above. When an etiology is determined (i.e. not idiopathic), what is the most common cause of this fundus finding?
explanation: This patient’s presentation is suggestive of an acute left optic neuropathy given his vision loss, decreased color vision, and left afferent pupillary defect. The fundus findings are classic for neuroretinitis showing a swollen left optic nerve along with prominent macular exudates forming a “macular star.” While neuroretinitis can be harbinger of serious systemic disease and these entities should be ruled out with blood work, the majority of cases are idiopathic. When a cause is identified, the most common causative pathogen is Bartonella henselae. This gram negative rod is often transmitted via cat bites or cat scratches and often leads to “cat scratch fever” which can have protean manifestations including fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, endocarditis, and encephalopathy. Despite the potential for serious manifestations, the disease is self-limited unless the patient is immunocompromised. Treatment of neuroretinitis has never been proven to be beneficial although some practitioners will treat with doxycycline or rifampin. Interestingly, many patients with laboratory proven Bartonella henselae infection do not recall a cat scratch / bite. Some other known causes / associations with neuroretinitis include sarcoidosis, syphilis, Epstein-Barr virus, Lyme disease, histoplasmosis, toxocariasis, and toxoplasmosis. When a work-up fails to reveal an etiology, the term Leber’s idiopathic stellate neuroretinitis is sometimes used. explanation: The fundus photo depicts a unifocal area of chorioretinal inflammation adjacent to an old chorioretinal scar. In addition, there is adjacent optic nerve swelling and macular edema. These findings are typical for toxoplasmosis chorioretinitis which is the most common cause of posterior uveitis in the world (~one-fourth of cases of posterior uveitis in the United States). The classic initial therapy is with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and folinic acid. Topical steroids and cycloplegic drops also can be used for the anterior segment inflammation but will not quell the posterior uveitis. Oral prednisone can be started a few days (classically 3 days) after antibiotic therapy.
