He has been on HAART therapy for the past 5 years. On dilated fundus exam, you note the presence of a few cotton-wool spots without associated hemorrhages (see image). These lesions are approximately 100 microns in diameter. There is no vitreous cell. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of management for this patient?

question: There is no vitreous cell. Which of the following is the most appropriate course of management for this patient?

options.C: induction therapy with intravenous ganciclovir or foscarnet
options.A: Serial dilated fundus exams and photographs

explanation: Given that the patient's CD4 count is greater than 200 cells/mm3 and is on HAART therapy, it is unlikely that these white lesions represent cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis. Instead, this patient most likely just has HIV retinopathy (microangiopathy) which is typically asymptomatic and requires no treatment. However, it is prudent to follow any retinal lesions in HIV patients to ensure there is no change over time especially if the patient's CD4 count is low. In contrast, CMV retinitis has the following characteristics: • Patients typically have CD4 count less than 50 cells/mm3. • Mild vitreous and/or anterior chamber inflammation. • Three clinical forms: o "Pizza or cottage cheese with ketchup retinopathy" -- confluent areas of retinal necrosis with hemorrhages in the posterior pole. These lesions eventually enlarge and merge together and can lead to retinal obliterative detachment. Optic disc edema may be present. o Indolent form. This type is characterized by granular peripheral retinal lesions with little or no hemorrhages. o Frosted branch angiitis. This type is characterized by marked vascular sheathing. It is less common than the other two forms. • Initially, the lesions may resemble cotton-wool spots, but CMV lesions are typically >500-750 microns in size (cotton-wool spots are typically <500 microns in diameter). WRONG ANSWERS: • Choice B: obtaining CMV serologies would not be helpful since most people in the general population are CMV positive. • Choice C: since it is unlikely that this patient has CMV retinitis, there is no indication to starting CMV medications for this patient. • Choice D: there is no role for laser demarcation in HIV microangiopathy. The fundus findings are classic for neuroretinitis showing a swollen left optic nerve along with prominent macular exudates forming a "macular star." When a cause of neuroretinitis is identified (most are idiopathic), the most common causative pathogen is Bartonella henselae. This gram negative rod is often transmitted via cat bites or cat scratches and can lead to "cat scratch fever" with many possible manifestations including fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatitis, endocarditis, and encephalopathy. The natural history of neuroretinitis is development of swelling of the optic nerve head with extravasation of subretinal / intraretinal serous fluid. question: • A 55-year-old man is referred to you for a hazy vitreous and "milky" lesions in the posterior pole of the left eye (see image above). He has a recent medical history of being hospitalized for the past 4 weeks after an abdominal surgery. You perform a diagnostic pars plana vitrectomy to obtain the correct diagnosis. Your other workup reveals no systemic involvement. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate treatment for this disease entity and presentation?
explanation: The fundus photo depicts "fluffy" yellow-white lesions that appear to be projecting into the vitreous. Given the appearance of these lesions and the patient's prolonged hospitalization, one has to worry about endogenous fungal endophthalmitis. Other risk factors for this condition include prolonged indwelling catheters, intravenous drug use, chronic antibiotic use, hyperalimentation, recent abdominal surgery, and diabetes. Endogenous fungal endophthalmitis is most commonly caused by Candida species. Diagnosis of this disease entity can sometimes be made on clinical grounds alone, especially if the patient has a known systemic Candida infection. However if systemic Candida infection is not present, a definitive diagnosis may require culture (or other test like PCR) of intraocular specimens (e.g. vitreous). This specimen is usually best obtained by pars plana vitrectomy instead of a random vitreous tap. Patients with endogenous Candida endophthalmitis localized to the choroid or retina and without systemic involvement can be treated with oral fluconazole or voriconazole. This treatment usually lasts at least 2 months. If the infection extends into the vitreous (as in this case), then intravitreal antifungals and/or pars plana vitrectomy + intravitreal amphotericin or voriconazole is added to the aforementioned systemic anti-fungal treatment. explanation: Zellweger syndrome is the most severe of the three diseases that constitute the "Zellweger spectrum". The three diseases are (from least to most severe): (1) infantile Refsum's; (2) neonatal adrenoleukodystrophy; and (3) Zellweger syndrome. The "Zellweger spectrum" is itself a subgroup of diseases under the broader category of "peroxisome biogenesis disorders" (PBD). Individuals with Zellweger's syndrome do not typically live past the first 6 months of life. In addition, mild-to-severe temporal optic atrophy may also be seen in this condition (as seen especially in the photo of the right eye). explanation: There are two main groups of "hereditary hyaloideoretinopathies with optically empty vitreous" -- those with ocular signs exclusively and those with other systemic manifestations. Those with solely ocular signs include Jansen and Wagner disease. Those with other systemic signs include Stickler syndrome, "hereditary arthro-ophthalmopathy with stiff joints" (Weill-Marchesani variety), and variants with dwarfism. Stickler syndrome is the most common of these hyaloideoretinopathies. It is an autosomal dominant collagen disorder and the most commonly affected gene is COL2A1. Recall that type 2 collagen is present in vitreous, synovial fluid, and cartilage. Up to 60% of affected patients develop retinal detachments and 90% develop retinal tears due to premature vitreous breakdown, high myopia (>90%), and radial pigmented (perivascular) lattice degeneration. Prophylactic laser should be considered for extensive lattice, especially in high risk patients with a prior history of a retinal detachment in the fellow eye. Slit lamp examination will reveal abnormal vitreous that appears "optically empty" and liquefied. Subcortical cataracts can be seen. Stickler syndrome is often associated with systemic findings, such as facial abnormalities (e.g., Pierre Robin, cleft palate), joint hypermobility, hearing loss, and osteoarthritis. question: A 22-year-old woman presents to your office with complaints of seeing a "dark spot" in the center of both eyes. Her visual acuity is 20/40 OD and 20/50 OS. She has small paracentral scotomas on Amsler grid testing. On dilated fundus exam, you note the pathology as seen in the photograph above. Mutations of which of the following genes is most likely involved?
explanation: The fundus photo shows foveal atrophy surrounded by yellowish, "pisciform flecks" at the level of the retinal pigment epithelium. These fundus findings are characteristic for Stargardt disease. A fluorescein angiogram may demonstrate the phenomenon of a "dark choroid" which is rather specific to Stargardt disease. Most cases of Stargardt's are autosomal recessive in inheritance and are caused by mutations in the ABCA4 gene. Mutations in the RDS/peripherin (currently aka PRPH2) gene cause different types of pattern dystrophy; mutations in VMD2 (currently aka BEST-1) are responsible for Best's disease; and mutations in TIMP3 are responsible for Sorsby's macular dystrophy. Q-Which of the following is the most common cause of vision loss in idiopathic juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasia, group 1?

question: Which of the following is the most common cause of vision loss in idiopathic juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasia, group 1?
explanation: Idiopathic juxtafoveal retinal telangiectasia (IJFT) refers to a heterogeneous group of disorders characterized by telangiectatic alterations of the juxtafoveolar capillary network of one or both eyes. IJFT was classically divided into 3 groups by Gass and Blodi1: Group 1 • Unilateral • Second most common type of IJFT • Occurs mainly in males • Vision loss mainly due to macular edema • Considered to be a congenital disorder (but presents clinically in middle- age) • Telangiectatic retinal capillaries and aneurysmal dilations are easily-seen on biomicroscopy. Some experts believe this is macular variant of Coat's disease. • Typically, these abnormalities are temporal to the fovea Group 2 • Most common form of IJFT • Bilateral • Occurs in middle-aged men and women • Presents with telangiectasias that are more difficult to see on ophthalmoscopy. Golden crystals and intra- and subretinal pigmented plaques may occur. • Vision loss due to retinal atrophy and subretinal neovascularization. The foveolar atrophy can resemble a lamellar macular hole. • Considered to be acquired Group 3 • Very rare • Progressive obliteration of the perifoveal capillary network • Typically has an associated systemic condition (e.g. CNS abnormalities) Each of these Groups has two subtypes ("A" and "B"), the description of which is beyond the scope of this website and most board exams. Click here for a nice table describing these different groups and their sub-types. The first vascular sign of IJRT group 2 is proliferation of the deep capillary plexus in the temporal juxtafovea retina. There is also loss of transparency of the retina in the temporal juxtafoveal area. • Stage 2 (superficial capillary). The telangiectatic proliferation begins to involve the inner capillary plexus. There are anastomoses between this inner capillary plexus and the deep capillary plexus. Multiple microaneurysms may be seen which may leak on fluorescein angiogram. However, this leakage does not typically result in edema within the inner retina (i.e. no CME). • Stage 3 (subinternal limiting membrane). The vasogenic process extends into the subinternal limiting membrane and also through the retina posteriorly to the retinal pigment epithelium. Eventually, this process extends around the perifoveal area. • Stage 4 (proliferative). A subretinal neovascularization then can form when the vasogenic process extends below the retina. This form of neovascularization is indistinguishable from a choroidal neovascularization (e.g. from macular degeneration). • Stage 5 (fibrovascular proliferation). Eventually, some of these eyes will end up with a fibrovascular proliferation/scar. explanation: Rod monochromatism is an autosomal recessive inherited retinal disorder of the cone system leading to dysfunction of the cone photoreceptors. The disease is stationary and presents in infancy with nystagmus that may improve with age, photophobia, and decreased visual acuity. Visual acuity typically is worse than 20/100. There may be a paradoxical pupillary response (pupil constriction with transitioning from light to dark) and hyperopia is common. Some patients have an incomplete form with some cone function and residual color vision. Diagnosis is based on specialized color testing and ERG findings. Dark-adapted (DA) rod responses to a dim stimulus are normal, and to a bright stimulus can be normal or show mild attenuation of the a- and b-waves representing the loss of the cone system's contribution. However, photopic, light-adapted (LA) responses are typically completely undetectable from loss of the cone system. Fundus examination may be normal or show subtle granularity of the fovea, and this can be progressive. OCT of the foveola is often abnormal showing disruption of the ellipsoid zone, and a majority of patients have foveal hypoplasia. WRONG ANSWERS • (Choice A): Blue-cone monochromatism (BCM) is a stationary inherited disease of the cone system that results in selective loss the L ("red")- and M ("green")-cones but with preserved S ("blue")-cones. The condition can present similarly to rod monochromatism in infancy with nystagmus, photophobia, and decreased visual acuity. Unlikely rod monochromatism, BCM shows x-linked recessive inheritance, visual acuity is typically better (ranging from 20/80 to 20/200), and the majority of patients are myopic. Specialized color testing as well as ERG findings will further distinguish the two disorders. • (Choice B, C): Fundus albipunctatus and Oguchi disease are two congenital night-blinding disorders that have abnormal fundus findings. This is in contrast to congenital stationary night blindness (CSNB) which has a normal fundus. All of these disorders are stationary inherited disorders of the rod system that present with nyctalopia. Fundus albipunctatus individuals show yellow-white dots that spare the fovea and extend into the midperiphery. It is due to mutations in the RDH5 gene which encodes an RPE protein necessary for rhodopsin regeneration leading to delayed rhodopsin regeneration in dark-adapted conditions. ERG responses demonstrate preserved cone function. ERG DA responses may normalize with extended dark adaptation due to the delayed rhodopsin regeneration. Oguchi disease has a peculiar fundus finding where the fundus appears normal after dark adaptation but develops a yellow sheen after brief light exposure, known as the Mizuo-Nakamura phenomenon). Patients with Fundus albipunctatus and Oguchi disease usually have normal visual acuity, color vision, and visual fields. explanation: Best disease is an autosomal dominant disease caused by mutations in the VMD2 gene (aka as the BEST 1 gene). This gene encodes the protein, "bestrophin", which is a transmembrane chloride channel located in the basolateral membrane of the RPE. Individuals with Best disease show a yellow, yolk-like (vitelliform) macular lesion in childhood which eventually breaks down into an atrophic appearance (i.e. "scrambled egg yolk"). Despite the prominent appearance of the macular lesion, these individuals surprisingly maintain good visual acuity in the majority of the cases. Approximately 20% of these patients will develop a choroidal neovascular membrane which reduces vision to the 20/200 level. Another pearl to remember about Best disease is that the ERG is typically normal while the EOG is always abnormal (i.e. Arden ratio < 1.5). explanation: The fundus photo shows a mild, lightly-pigmented fundus. The foveal reflex is also not distinct in this photo. The patient also has cutaneous and hair hypopigmentation; therefore, he has some form of oculocutaneous albinism. Since he apparently has not gained more pigment over the years, he most likely has tyrosinase-negative oculocutaneous albinism. The terms "complete" versus "partial" albinism and "tyrosinase-negative" versus "tyrosinase- positive" albinism have been replaced with a classification scheme based on the specific gene mutation. Regardless, the BCSC still discusses how individuals with tyrosinase-positive oculocutaneous albinism will have slow darkening of their skin, hair, irides, and RPE over time. The BCSC also states that this progressively- increased pigmentation is associated with improved nystagmus and visual acuity over time. This teenager should not be classified as having ocular albinism since he also has skin/hair involvement. Regardless of whether an individual has oculocutaneous albinism or ocular albinism, his/her ocular involvement may follow one of two clinical patterns: true albinism or albinoidism. "Albinoidism" is a generic term used to describe a milder clinical pattern of ocular involvement. "Albinoidism" confers milder visual consequences with normal development of the fovea while "true albinism" implies poor vision with a hypoplastic fovea (e.g. loss of foveal pit/reflex and non evident luteal pigment). The gold standard for diagnosing true albinism is flash and pattern VEPs (visual evoked potentials). Both of these ocular clinical pattners share the features of photophobia, iris transillumination defects, and hypopigmented fundi. Interestingly, the temporal nerve fibers decussate instead of projecting to the ipsilateral lateral geniculate body in all forms of albinism. As discussed in a separate question in this section, one should inquire about other systemic symptoms when a patient is diagnosed with albinism. Such systemic symptoms may be the harbinger of serious diseases associated with albinism like Chédiak-Higashi syndrome or Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome. explanation: The fundus photo shows well-defined and bilaterally symmetric central areas of atrophy which affect the RPE and choriocapillaris. As a result, the large choroidal vessels are readily seen underneath. In older patients, this appearance could simulate the geographic atrophy that occurs in some age-related degeneration patients. However, given the apparent autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, age of onset in middle age, lack of abnormalities on electrophysiologic studies, and relatively normal choroidal flush, this patient most likely has central areolar choroidal dystrophy (CACD). CACD is caused by mutations in the peripherin/RDS gene (PRPH2) and is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern (although some autosomal recessive cases have been reported). The age of onset is in the 30-60 years of age and the presenting visual acuity is typically in the 20/25 to 20/200 range. Early fundus findings include a mild degree of nonspecific granularity of the fovea which slowly progresses to the pathognomonic round zone of neurosensory, RPE, and choriocapillary atrophy seen above. Unlike Best's disease, where the EOG is always abnormal, electrophysiologic studies are normal in CACD except in advanced cases. Unlike Stargardt's disease which presents with a diffusely-"silent choroid" on FA, the choroidal flush is mostly normal in CACD. Also, inheritance in Stargardt's is usually in an autosomal recessive pattern. Patients with North Carolina macular dystrophy typically reach their final visual acuity (~20/50-20/200) by late puberty, which contrasts the later onset of CACD. explanation: The vignette is alluding to the condition known as fundus albipunctatus (FA). This is a rare, hereditary, and typically stationary retinal disease. It is characterized by the following attributes: • Many small white/yellow lesions distributed throughout the retina except the fovea. • Normal optic discs and retinal vessels (unlike retinitis pigmentosa). • Visual acuity, visual fields, and color vision are typically normal (unless a dim stimulus is used). A dim environment will cause worsening of visual acuity and a constriction of the visual field. • Rod electroretinogram (ERG) is minimal but normalizes after the patient spends several hours in a dark environment. • Non-progressive. FA is typically inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. The vast majority of cases are caused by mutations in the RDH5 gene which encodes 11-cis retinol dehydrogenase, which is located in the retinal pigment epithelium and is involved in the visual cycle (i.e. regeneration of the visual pigment, rhodopsin). The main differential diagnosis of FA is retinitis punctata albescens (RPA). Though they have similar (confusing) names, they are completely different entities. Though both conditions can feature yellow/white dots, retinitis punctata albescens is a varient of retinitis pigmentosa and thus also features narrowed retinal vessels, optic disc pallor, and a severely-depressed ERG that does not recover with dark adaptation. Visual acuity and fields are progressively affected with RPA and the fundus in older individuals can have other hallmarks of retinitis pigmentosa like bone spicules. RPA is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner and is caused by mutations in the RLBP1 gene (retinaldehyde binding protein 1) which is also involved in the visual cycle. Mutations in this gene can also rarely cause some forms of FA. Mutations in the ABCA4 gene are responsible for most cases of Stargardt disease. Other diseases associated with mutations in this gene include cone-rod dystrophy, retinitis pigmentosa, and fundus flavimaculatus (variant of Stargardt). Mutations in the RDS/peripherin gene are typically associated with the pattern dystrophies (e.g. adult-onset foveomacular vitelliform dystrophy, butterfly dystrophy). explanation: The photo on the left shows macular pigment mottling while the photo on the right shows polydactyly. This teenager is also obese and his vision difficulties began with night vision. These findings and history are most consistent with a diagnosis of Bardet-Biedl syndrome (BBS). Individuals with BBS may also have a pigmentary retinopathy that resembles retinitis pigmentosa (RP), albeit usually without classic bone-spicules. They typically begin with night vision problems, then peripheral vision problems, and finally also with central vision loss by early adulthood. Other key features of BBS are intellectual disability, hypogonadism, and renal failure There is some overlap between BBS and Laurence-Moon syndrome (LMS) and some authors consider them to be on the continuum of the same syndrome. Classically however, LMS features spastic paraplegia and does NOT have polydactyly. Alström syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder chararacterized by a tapetoretinal degeneration, obesity, diabetes, hearing loss, renal failure, and dilated cardiomyopathy. Unlike the other pigmentary retinopathies, central vision is lost early in Alström syndrome. Unlike BBS, there is no polydactyly, hypogonadism, or intellectual disability in these patients. question: What is the characteristic fluorescein angiography finding in Stargardt disease?
explanation: Stargardt disease, or fundus flavimaculatus, is an inherited juvenile cone-rod dystrophy that causes progressive vision loss with final visual acuity ranging from 20/50-20/200. The progression usually starts between the ages of six and twelve years old; the rate of progression is quite variable. The characteristic fundus appearance in Stargardt disease includes yellow parafoveal “pisciform” flecks with peripapillary sparing and a “beaten bronze” macula. Present in about 80% of cases and a very specific finding, a dark choroid is believed to be a blocking phenomena whereby lipofuscin-like material accumulates in the retinal pigment epithelial layer and prevents transmission of fluorescence from the choroid below. Fluorescein quenching is an idiopathic rapid clearing of fluorescein in patients with Birdshot chorioretinopathy. Expansile dot leakage from the choriocapillaris into the subretinal space occurs in central serous chorioretinopathy (along with the “chimney stack” leakage pattern). Patchy, delayed choroidal filling is typical of choroidal ischemia in giant cell arteritis although can occur in other choroidopathies such as hypertensive choroidopathy or Wegener granulomatosis-associated choroidopathy. • Q-A 25-year-old patient with a history of autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa presents with decreased central vision OS over the last month. explanation: Choroideremia is an X-linked recessive disease which is caused by mutations of the CHM gene. This gene encodes for a geranylgeranyl transferase Rab escort protein. The general progression of fundus changes is: • Starts as mottled areas of pigmentation in the anterior equatorial region and macula. • These affected anterior areas degenerate to confluent scalloped areas of RPE and choriocapillaris loss. • There is typically no change in the retinal vasculature or optic atrophy. The differential diagnosis of choroideremia is gyrate atrophy, Bietti crystalline dystrophy, and thioridazine retinal toxicity. Histologic studies have localized the CHM gene product to the RPE. Therefore, the basic defect in this disease involves the RPE (not the choriocapillaris). Most patients with this disease maintain good visual acuity for 4 or 5 decades. There is no known treatment for choroideremia though gene therapy holds some future promise. Carriers of the CHM mutation are typically asymptomatic and have normal ERG results. However, carriers often show patches of subretinal black mottled pigment or a lobular pattern of RPE and choriocapillaris loss. explanation: Perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) is most commonly employed during repair of complex retinal detachments such as those due to giant retinal tears or complicated by proliferative vitreoretinopathy. Properties of PFCL that contribute to its usefulness include: • High specific gravity relative to saline, resulting in excellent retinal tamponade • Low viscosity, allowing easy injection and removal • High boiling point, avoiding vaporization with endophotocoagulation during surgery • High surface tension, allowing the liquid to remain as a single bubble Subfoveal retained perfluorocarbon liquid (PFCL) is a rare but serious complication associated with retinal detachment repair. Optical coherence tomography reveals characteristic large hyporeflective spaces corresponding to retained PFCL bubbles. PFCL is toxic when in direct contact with the retina for prolonged periods and subfoveal PFCL may result in permanent vision loss. question: Where is the causative break most likely to be found?

options.D: at the 6 o'clock position or within one-and-a-half clock hours to either side of 6 o'clock
options.C: within one-and-a-half clock hours of the highest border of the RD
options.B: within one-and-a-half clock hours of the lowest border of the RD
options.A: at the 12 o'clock position or within one-and-a-half clock hours to either side of 12 o'clock

explanation: • "Lincoff's rules" help localize the causative retinal break in the case of a rhegmatogenous RD. Rule #1: for superior temporal or nasal RDs, the primary break lies within one- and-a-half clock hours of the highest border of the RD. Rule #2: for total or superior RDs that cross the 12 o'clock, the primary break is at 12 o'clock or in a triangle (the apex of which is at the ora serrata and where the sides extend one-and-a-half clock hours to either side). Rule #3: for inferior RDs, the higher side of the RD indicates on which side of the optic disc the primary break is located. Rule #4: for "inferior" **bullous** RDs, the primary break is located superiorly. explanation: The BEAT-ROP study was a multicenter, randomized clinical trial that compared retinal ablative treatment with intravitreal bevacizumab monotherapy in 150 subjects with zone I or zone II posterior stage 3 with plus disease retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). Retinopathy of prematurity recurred in 4 infants in the bevacizumab group (6 of 140 eyes [4%]) and 19 infants in the laser-therapy group (32 of 146 eyes [22%]). A significant treatment effect was found for zone I retinopathy of prematurity (P=0.003) but not for zone II disease (P=0.27). The researchers concluded that intravitreal bevacizumab monotherapy, as compared with conventional laser therapy, in infants with stage 3+ retinopathy of prematurity showed a significant benefit for zone I but not zone II disease. This study established intravitreal bevacizumab monotherapy as an effective alternative to conventional laser therapy in select high-risk ROP infants. explanation: The two strongest risk factors for the development of retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) are gestational age (GA) and birth weight (BW). The importance of these two risk factors is reflected in the American Academy of Ophthalmology and American Academy of Pediatrics' guidelines which state that all infants ≤30 weeks of GA or ≤1,500 grams of BW should be screened for ROP. Another major risk factor for the development of severe ROP is the use of supplemental oxygen. However, though decreased supplemental oxygen use decreases the incidence of ROP, it also results in higher infant morbidity and mortality. Beyond those three major risk factors, many other factors increase the incidence of ROP: • Respiratory distress disorder (RDS). This condition is caused by a surfactant deficiency in the neonate. The increased incidence of ROP in neonates with RDS is logical since these infants require mechanical ventilation and supplemental oxygen use. • Transfusion of red blood cells. Many studies support that the need for blood transfusions is a risk factor for ROP. However, there is conflicting evidence whether anemia itself is an independent risk factor. • Thrombocytopenia. • Neonatal sepsis. • Low postnatal weight gain. Slow weight gain is also associated with a lower postnatal increase of serum insulin growth factor-1 (IGF-1). IGF-1 is a hormone that promotes the development of several tissues including retinal vessels. There is conflicting evidence whether or not male gender increases the rate of ROP. Caffeine is commonly administered for the treatment and prophylaxis of apnea of prematurity. There are several studies that have found that severe ROP was less common in infants assigned to caffeine. explanation: The CRYO-ROP study was a multicenter, randomized clinical trial that compared cryotherapy retinal ablative treatment in the study eye with observation of the fellow eye in 172 subjects with threshold retinopathy of prematurity (ROP). Threshold disease was defined as five or more contiguous or eight cumulative clock hours of stage 3 ROP in zone 1 or 2 in the presence of "plus" disease. An unfavorable outcome was defined as posterior retinal detachment, retinal fold involving the macula, or retrolental tissue. Unfavorable outcomes were significantly less in the eyes that underwent cryotherapy (21.8%) compared with the untreated eyes (43%). This study defined threshold ROP and established peripheral retinal ablation as the standard of care in subjects with threshold ROP. If OCT imaging were to be obtained through the finding, which of the following layers would be abnormal?

question: If OCT imaging were to be obtained through the finding, which of the following layers would be abnormal?
explanation: The finding in the photo is commotio retinae. In the setting of blunt trauma to the front of the eye, the retina can develop a gray-white discoloration due to damage to the outer retinal layers, specifically the photoreceptors and RPE. Affected areas may be confined to the posterior pole causing decreased vision or involve extensive areas of peripheral retina with no visual symptoms. The outer retinal whitening will resolve over weeks and may leave no abnormal fundus findings, or may cause mottling of the RPE, pigment migration, or rarely full-thickness macular hole formation if in the posterior pole. Recovery of the affected cells range from complete recovery to contusion necrosis causing outer retinal atrophy and loss of the RPE. Fluorescein angiography initially reveals no alterations in retinal or choroidal perfusion in the area of commotio but may show staining of the RPE. Later, window defects may be present due to RPE atrophy. Acutely, OCT shows increased reflectivity and disruption of the photoreceptor layers followed by either loss of the photoreceptors and RPE or complete normalization of the OCT depending on the extent of the injury. WRONG ANSWERS: • (Choice A, C): The inner retina is not affected in commotio retinae. A clue in this case is the normal appearance of the retinal vasculature overlying the area of retinal whitening. • (Choice D): The choriocapillaris typically exhibits no abnormalities on multimodal imaging after development of commotio retinae. explanation: There are 3 basic mechanisms by which light can damage the retina: (1) mechanical; (2) thermal; and (3) photochemical. Mechanical damage occurs when the absorbed light is strong enough to produce gas bubbles that result in a shock wave to mechanically disrupt tissues. YAG capsulotomy is an example of light energy causing mechanical damage. Thermal damage is when absorbed light causes a rise in temperature of surrounding tissues. Laser photocoagulation (e.g. panretinal photocoagulation) is an application of this type of damage. Photochemical damage is when light induces biochemical reactions that cause tissue destruction without a rise in temperature. explanation: The clinical vignette is classic for commotio retinae which often complicates blunt trauma to the eye. Originally, commotio retinae was thought to be caused by retinal edema (i.e. extracellular accumulation of fluid). Thus, the previous term of "Berlin edema." However, this cause of retinal whitening now has been found to be caused by disruption in the architecuture of the photoreceptor elements. Commotio retinae is most commonly found in the macula, but can occur anywhere in the retina. When it involves the macula, it can appear as a "cherry red spot" since the cells involved in the whitening are not present in the fovea. Visual prognosis is typically good with the commotio resolving over 3-4 weeks. However, it may be complicated by choroidal rupture, macular pigmentary changes, and macular hole formation. Answer "C" is alluding to the pathological changes underlying a cotton-wool spot (CWS). The most common cause of a CWS is diabetes. Thus, even the presence of one CWS, in a patient without any known medical conditions, should prompt a systemic workup (e.g. hemoglobin A1c, glucose tolerance test, blood pressure measurement). Answer "D" is alluding to the cause underlying myelinated nerve fiber layer. Typically, myelination of nerve fibers in the optic pathway stops at the lamina cribosa. However occasionally, the myelination can extend past the lamina cribosa. This is a congenital cause of retinal whitening. It is typically contiguous with the optic nerve head, but occasionally can occur away from it. Myelinated nerve fiber layer can occasionally cause significant amblyopia and even a scotoma. Q-What is the most common hereditary hyaloideoretinopathy?

question: What is the most common hereditary hyaloideoretinopathy?
explanation: The hereditary hyaloideoretinopathies are a group of disorders marked by an “optically empty vitreous cavity” on examination due to premature vitreous breakdown. These disorders also have a high incidence of retinal detachment thought to be related to scattered lattice and thinning of the retina (excluding Wagner disease which does not have a predilection for retinal detachment). Other ocular abnormalities including cataract, myopia, glaucoma and strabismus are more common in these disorders compared to normal eyes. Some hereditary hyaloideoretinopathies such as Jansen disease and Wagner disease have no associated systemic features while Stickler syndrome is associated with skeletal abnormalities including facial dysgenesis in a pattern known as Pierre Robin sequence with micrognathia (small jaw), cleft palate, and glossoptosis (downward displacement of the tongue). Other skeletal pathology associated with Stickler syndrome includes hyperflexible joints and arthritis. Stickler syndrome is transmitted in an autosomal dominant fashion and is caused by a mutation in the gene encoding type II procollagen. Marfan syndrome is not regarded to be a hereditary hyaloideoretinopathy. Q-A 60-year-old woman is referred to you with decreased vision and increased intraocular pressure (IOP) in both eyes. explanation: All of the answer choices represent genes where mutations in them can cause a form of amyloidosis. "Amyloidosis" is a generic term that is used to describe the deposition of fibrils which are composed of low molecular weight (5 to 25 kD) subunits of a variety of proteins. Many of these proteins are normal substances found in the serum. These fibrils undergo an abnormal conformational change into the classic antiparallel beta-pleated sheet. These abnormal proteins deposit into various organs within the body causing their dysfunction. All these protein aggregates classically stain with Congo Red and show apple-green birefringence with dichroism under polarized light. There are at least 30 different human protein precursors which can result in "amyloidosis." A full discussion of all the various forms of amyloidosis are well beyond the scope of this website. However, there are only a few forms of amyloidosis that you really need to remember since they involve the eye: Mutations in the transthyretin (TTR) gene • The TTR gene is located on chromosome 18. Transthyretin was previously known as prealbumin. • Though >120 TTR mutations have been described, the most common ones cause something called "familial amyloid polyneuropathy (FAP) types I and II". • Systemic manifestations include upper/lower extremity polyneuropathy, central nervous system abnormalities, cardiomyopathy, carpal tunnel syndrome, and gastrointestinal/renal abnormalities. • Classic ocular manifestation: bilateral vitreous opacification associated with retinal hemorrhages/exudates/cotton-wool spots, and peripheral retinal neovascularization. The vitreous opacities are classically described as "glass-wool." • These patients with transthyretin-related familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy commonly develop increased IOP. • In contrast to other causes of vitreous opacities like asteroid hyalosis, vitreous infiltration by amyloidosis is frequently visually significant. used by transthyretin mutations, also commonly presents with increased intraocular pressure. Mutations in the keratoepithelin (TGFBI) gene • Many corneal dystrophies are associated with different mutations in the TGFBI gene including: Reis-Bucklers, Thiel-Behnke, granular corneal dystrophy type 1, lattice corneal dystrophy type 1 (LCD1), Avellino corneal dystrophy (aka granular type 2). • These corneal dystrophies are considered forms of "primary localized amyloidosis" since there are no systemic manifestations and only the cornea is involved. Mutations in the gelsolin (GSN) gene • Result in what is called "lattice corneal dystrophy, gelsolin type" (which is actually not a "true" corneal dystrophy since there are systemic manifestations). • Also called "lattice corneal dystrophy type 2" (LCD 2); Meretoja's syndrome; familial amyloidosis, Finnish (FAF); amyloidosis V; and familial amyloidotic polyneuropathy IV (FAP-IV). • Systemic features include: masked facies, dermatochalasis, lagophthalmos, pendulous ears, dry/lax skin, and cranial and peripheral nerve palsies. Other possible manifestations include orthostatic hypotension, cardiac conduction abnormalities, and problems with perspiration. Also, the incidence of glaucoma is increased in LCD2 (which is not a feature of LCD1). The main distinguishing corneal features of LCD2 are that there are fewer lattice lines which are more radially-oriented and involve more of the peirpheral cornea compared to LCD1. The central cornea is relatively spared and there are less amorphous dots compared to LCD1. Q-You are examining an otherwise-healthy patient with a remote history of ocular trauma to his right eye. Q-A 65-year old patient undergoes pars plana vitrectomy for an epiretinal membrane. What is this patient's approximate risk of developing a visually-significant cataract within the next 2 years?

question: What is this patient's approximate risk of developing a visually-significant cataract within the next 2 years?
explanation: The most common complication after vitrectomy surgery is the development of a visually-significant cataract. According to the BCSC Retina book, >90% of eyes in patients over age 50 will develop visually significant nuclear sclerotic cataract within 2 years of vitrectomy surgery. Another noteworthy complication noted by the BCSC is the increased long-term risk of open-angle glaucoma (~10-20%) after vitrectomy. Dr. Stanley Chang's seminal work (published in the American Journal of Ophthalmology) on this subject found the following: • Among pre-op glaucoma suspects, the mean IOP was 19.5 ± 2.7 mm Hg in the vitrectomized eye, compared with 14.3 ± 3.0 mm Hg in the fellow eye (p = .0001). • Among eyes where glaucoma only developed after vitrectomy, the time interval between vitrectomy and the diagnosis of glaucoma was significantly longer (45.95 ± 44.79 months) in phakic eyes compared to nonphakic eyes (18.39 ± 13.76 months) (p = .0115). In other words, presence of the lens appeared protective against glaucoma. • Among eyes already being treated for glaucoma pre-op, the mean number of glaucoma medications was higher (2.9 ± 1.2) in the vitrectomized eye compared to the fellow (non-vitrectomized) eye (2.00 ± 1.4; p = .0215). It is most commonly employed during repair of complex retinal detachments such as those due to giant retinal tears or complicated by proliferative vitreoretinopathy. Subfoveal retained PFCL is a rare but serious complication associated with retinal detachment repair. Optical coherence tomography reveals characteristic large hyporeflective spaces corresponding to retained PFCL bubbles. PFCL is toxic when in direct contact with the retina for prolonged periods and subfoveal PFCL may result in permanent vision loss. As such, the recommended treatment option is repeat vitrectomy and evacuation of the bubbles. Topical NSAIDs and topical or intravitreal steroids may be useful in post-operative cystoid macular edema but are not useful in the case of subfoveal PFCL. Therefore the classic choice for imaging in this scenario is FA because the blue light entering the eye is scattered but the resulting fluorescence of the fluorescein in the veins comes from the opposite direction of the detector (camera) and therefore the obtained images is free of scatter and reflection. question: You are examining a 30-year-old man in the intensive care unit. This patient was involved in an auto accident 3 days ago and subsequently underwent emergency craniotomy for a subarachnoid hemorrhage. His fundus exam is significant for the findings seen above. Similar findings were found in the left eye as well. What is the proposed mechanism for these ocular findings?

options.D: acute rise in intraocular venous pressure
options.C: acute compression of the choroidal vessels
options.A: occlusion of small arterioles especially near the peripapillary retina

explanation: Terson syndrome is characterized by vitreous and sub-internal limiting membrane or sub-hyaloid hemorrhage caused by an acute intracranial hemorrhage. The proposed mechanism for these multi-level hemorrhages is that the acute intracranial hemorrhage causes an acute rise in intraocular venous pressure. It is estimated that 1/3 of patients with subdural and subarachnoid hemorrhage have Terson syndrome. Typically, the hemorrhage associated with Terson syndrome clears spontaneously and visual function is not severely affected once the blood clears. The main condition that is differentiated from Terson syndrome after acute trauma is Purtscher retinopathy. In this latter condition, the fundus appearance is characterized by large cotton-wool spots, hemorrhages, and retinal edema most commonly surrounding the optic disc (see image below). Optic atrophy (and thus permanent vision loss) is more common in Purtscher retinopathy compared to Terson syndrome and is thought to be caused by injury-induced complement activation which results in granulocyte aggregation and leukoembolization. This cascade then occludes small arterioles, especially of the peripapillary retina. Other conditions that do not involve trauma can exhibit findings similar to Purtscher retinopathy. In these non-traumatic cases, the fundus findings are called "Purtscher- like" retinopathy. Causes of Purtscher-like retinopathy include: acute pancreatitis, collagen-vascular diseases, childbirth, and amniotic fluid embolism. Again, a similar mechanism of complement-mediated leukoembolization is thought to cause this retinopathy in non-traumatic cases. • A 45-year-old hyperopic man presents to your clinic for a routine eye exam. question: • A 45-year-old hyperopic man presents to your clinic for a routine eye exam. He offers no complaints. On dilated fundus exam, you note an abnormality in the inferotemporal quadrant of the right eye (see photos above). There is no vitreous hemorrhage or pigment or shifting fluid. Which of the following is TRUE regarding this condition?

options.D: on Humphrey visual field testing, there would be a relative, superonasal visual field defect
options.C: laser demarcation should be performed to prevent posterior extension
options.B: he should undergo an urgent pneumatic retinopexy or possible scleral buckling and/or pars plana vitrectomy procedure(s)
options.A: posterior extension is more common if the site of pathology is located in the nerve fiber layer

explanation: The fundus and red-free photos depict a bullous, "dome-shaped" elevation of the retina. These photos, along with the absence of vitreous hemorrhage/pigment, inferotemporal location, and absence of shifting fluid, are characteristics of degenerative retinoschisis. Retinoschisis is a splitting of the neurosensory retina which can resemble a retinal detachment. Other features that differentiate retinoschisis from a retinal detachment include: absolute scotoma, positive reaction to photocoagulation, and absence of corrugation. Degenerative retinoschisis is sometimes subdivided into typical and reticular forms. In typical degenerative retinoschisis, the splitting occurs in the outer plexiform layer while in reticular degenerative retinoschisis, the splitting occurs in the nerve fiber layer. Posterior extension of the schisis cavity is more common in the reticular form Retinal detachment can occur with retinoschisis, but it is a relatively rare occurrence. For example, previous studies have found retinoschisis to be present in 6% of rhegmatogenous retinal detachments (RRDs), but retinoschisis was only responsible for less than 2.5% of RRDs. In general, there are two patterns of retinal detachment that can occur with retinoschisis. The first pattern is a localized and stable form with outer retinal holes only. The second pattern is a symptomatic and rapidly-progressive detachment with both inner and outer layer holes. Only treatment for the latter type of retinal detachment is necessary. Prophylactic treatment is NOT recommended for asymptomatic patients with retinoschisis or with localized retinal detachments since complications can occur (e.g. new retinal breaks, vitreous hemorrhage). explanation: The prognosis for retinal reattachment is best for RDs caused by small holes or retinal dialyses and those associated with demarcation lines. It is worse for aphakic and pseudophakic eyes and the worst for RDs caused by PVR, giant tears, choroidal detachment, inflammation, and traumatic posterior breaks Q-Which of the following peripheral retinal abnormalities is associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment?

question: Which of the following peripheral retinal abnormalities is associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment?
explanation: Of the peripheral retinal lesions listed, only meridional folds (MFs) are associated with an increased risk of retinal detachment. MFs are folds of redundant peripheral retina that project into the vitreous. They are either aligned with a dentate process or with the middle of an ora bay. MFs are most commonly found in the superonasal quadrant. They are present in approximately 20% of all eyes. A meridional complex is when a dentate process and ciliary process occur within the same meridian. The involved dentate and ciliary processes are typically abnormally large, combined with a meridional fold, and usually associated with peripheral retinal excavation along the same meridian. Cobblestone degeneration describes small, discrete areas of atrophy of the outer retina. It is most common in the inferior quadrants and is present in approximately one-fifth of all people. The presence of cobblestone actually prevents the spread of a retinal detachment. Peripheral cystoid degeneration describes zones of microcysts in the far peripheral retina. It is present in nearly all adults. Q-Which of the following clinical features most strongly argues AGAINST the diagnosis of an exudative retinal detachment (RD)?

Q-An asymptomatic phakic 46-year-old female presents for evaluation. The images depict her condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for this condition?

question: An asymptomatic phakic 46-year-old female presents for evaluation. The images depict her condition. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for this condition?

options.C: Pars plana vitrectomy with endolaser and gas tamponade OD

explanation: The images depict degenerative retinoschisis. The OCT definitively demonstrates that this condition is retinoschisis and not a retinal detachment. Notice the split in the middle of the retina on the OCT. Degenerative retinoschisis is usually found in the inferotemporal quadrant in hyperopes and occurs bilaterally in 50-80% of affected patients. It may be divided into a typical and reticular subtype. The typical subtype has retinal splitting in the outer plexiform layer, while the reticular subtype has splitting in the nerve fiber layer. Retinal detachment and posterior extension is more common in the reticular form. Retinoschisis must have both inner and outer holes for a secondary retinal detachment to occur. A) Barrier laser retinopexy is appropriate when the retinoschisis is either threatening the macula or is associated with a secondary retinal detachment. Since this is not the case for this patient, this choice is not appropriate. B) Scleral buckling with cryotherapy would be an appropriate option for this patient if a secondary retinal detachment were present and the patient was symptomatic. Since this is not the case for this patient, this choice is not appropriate. C) Pars plana vitrectomy with endolaser and gas tamponade would be an option for this patient if a secondary retinal detachment were present and the patient was symptomatic. However, in this scenario, the patient's age and phakic status would make scleral buckling a more attractive option than vitrectomy. Since this is not the case for this patient, this choice is not appropriate. D) Observation is the best choice for this patient. The retinoschisis is the typical subtype as demonstrated by OCT and therefore is quite unlikely to extend posteriorly to threaten the macula in the future. question: Which of the following is a risk factor that may justify prophylactic laser demarcation of lattice degeneration?

options.D: history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye
options.A: presence of multiple atrophic holes within the lattice degeneration

explanation: Lattice degeneration, in the absence of risk factors, does not require prophylactic laser demarcation. An often-quoted, natural history study by Byer found a 1.08% chance of retinal detachment (RD) over 10.8 years in patients with lattice degeneration (0.7% of eyes). From this low incidence, Byer concluded that prophylactic treatment of lattice with or without holes in phakic, non-fellow eyes should be discontinued. However, the risk factors that may confer an increased risk of retinal detachment in eyes with lattice include: • high myopia • history of RD in the other eye • presence of flap tears within the lattice • aphakia (not pseudophakia) Q-A 29-year-old woman presents to you for a routine eye exam. explanation: Lattice degeneration occurs in ~6-10% of eyes, but is found in ~20-30% of eyes with a retinal detachment. Despite the latter fact, the risk of retinal detachment in untreated, asymptomatic, lattice degeneration patients is approximately 1%. Thus, the presence of lattice degeneration, even with atrophic holes, does not warrant prophylactic laser demarcation. However, certain risk factors may warrant the use of prophylactic laser for lattice degeneration. question: • Q-On dilated fundus examination, you note the presence of the retinal condition as depicted in the pathology photograph above. Which of the following features distinguishes this entity from a retinal detachment (RD)?
explanation: The photograph depicts senile retinoschisis. Retinoschisis can be differentiated from a rhegmatogenous RD by being: (a) smooth-domed; (b) absence of vitreous pigment or hemorrhage; (c) absolute scotoma; (d) reaction to photocoagulation; and (e) absence of shifting subretinal fluid. Retinoschisis typically occurs in the inferotemporal quadrant. Senile retinoschisis is currently divided into two types: "typical degenerative" and "reticular degenerative." The splitting of the retina occurs in the outer plexiform layer in typical degenerative retinoschisis while it occurs in the nerve fiber layer in reticular degenerative. Interestingly, senile retinoschisis is usually associated with hyperopia. Q-Which of the following peripheral retinal pathologies confers the LEAST risk of retinal detachment?

question: Which of the following peripheral retinal pathologies confers the LEAST risk of retinal detachment?

options.D: acute operculated retinal hole in a symptomatic patient
options.C: lattice degeneration in an aphakic patient
options.B: atrophic retinal hole in a phakic patient

explanation: Atrophic retinal holes are not typically associated with vitreoretinal traction and thus do not confer an increased risk of retinal detachment. These peripheral retinal lesions are often found incidentally and are estimated to occur in approximately 5% of the general population. They do not need to be treated with laser demarcation. Horseshoe retinal tears have a high incidence of progression to retinal detachment and should always be treated with prophylactic laser demarcation. The high risk is due to the almost universally-present vitreous traction along the edge of this flap tear. Individuals with lattice degeneration, with or without holes, do not typically need to be treated with prophylactic laser demarcation in the absence of other risk factors. However, if other risk factors exist (e.g. history of retinal detachment in the fellow eye; aphakia; flap tears), then these eyes should be lasered. Overall, operculated retinal holes have a lower risk of retinal detachment compared to horseshoe tears. However, many clinicians will laser barricade these lesions if they are symptomatic; if there is persistent vitreous traction at its margin; if the hole is large; or if the hole is superior in location. question: Which of the following types of retinal detachment is most closely associated with excessive panretinal photocoagulation (PRP)?
explanation: Excessive sessions of panretinal photocoagulation may elicit a great amount of chorioretinal edema and consequently cause retinal and choroidal detachment. This complication of PRP typically occurs a few days after the PRP session. Management usually consists of simply close observation with or without systemic corticosteroids. question: The top OCT image is abnormal and taken from the right eye of a patient with vision loss. The lower OCT image is taken from the normal left eye of the same patient. Which of the following diseases would be expected to result in the changes demonstrated in the right eye?
explanation: Multiple evanescent white dot syndrome (MEWDS) is a poorly understood, idiopathic inflammatory condition of the inner choroid and/or outer retina. It tends to occur unilaterally in younger myopic females and often presents with central vision loss, enlarged blind spot, and photopsias. Photopsias are very characteristic of MEWDS and other poorly understood inflammatory conditions such as acute zonal occult outer retinopathy (AZOOR) and idiopathic enlarged blind spot syndrome; photopsias as a prominent feature in a young patient with central vision loss should raise suspicion for these conditions. The hallmark features of MEWDS are short-lived white dots usually lasting from days to a week after visual symptoms begin, macular pigment stippling, macular wreath- like punctuate hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography, and mild disc edema in some cases. Recently with the advent of high quality spectral domain OCT (SD-OCT) images, it has been discovered that there are non-specific but characteristic outer segment and RPE changes on SD-OCT. Essentially the OCT shows disruption of the usual contour of these layers without evidence of retinal edema. Similar changes can be seen in AZOOR, commotio retinae, and solar retinopathy. In the correct clinical context, however, the disruption of the normal inner segment- outer segment and RPE layers is essentially diagnostic of MEWDS. This is helpful in cases such as this question where the white dots have long since resolved by the time the patient is examined. • Q-A 33-year-old man presents to your office with complaints of having "new blind spots" OS. However, the lesions in APMPPE resolve spontaneously over a few weeks and visual prognosis is generally good. In contrast, patients with serpiginous usually do poorly. In select cases, treatment with immunosuppressives (e.g. mycophenylate, cyclosporine, azathioprine, and prednisone) may induce remission. question: • Q-Which of the following features would be concerning for malignancy if seen on examination of this lesion?
explanation: The image above shows a hyperpigmented lesion with a vessel spanning superficially across the lesion suggesting that it is located in the deep retina or choroid. The appearance of this lesion is classic for a small choroidal nevus (diameter can be roughly inferred based on the adjacent blood vessels and is probably 0.5-1.5 disc diameters wide. The primary concern for any pigmented choroidal lesion is to ensure that it is not a melanoma. Features suggestive of melanoma rather than nevus include elevation of the lesion, width over 10 mm, overlying orange pigment clumping, adjacent sub- retinal fluid, visual symptoms from the lesion, and rapid growth on serial examinations. This lesion demonstrates none of these concerning features although if there is concern then the lesion should be followed over time with photographs to observe for rapid growth. When present, drusen overlying a choroidal hyperpigmented lesion is reassuring because it is a sign of chronicity and suggests the lesion is a benign nevus. Ultrasound can help distinguish a nevus from a melanoma in questionable causes because most choroidal nevi are less than 1 mm thick while most melanomas are more than 3 mm thick. Q-Which of the following is NOT a recommended management choice for an isolated choroidal hemangioma?

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended management choice for an isolated choroidal hemangioma?
explanation: Choroidal hemangiomas are benign and *never* metastasize. Therefore, systemic chemotherapy is never indicated. The most viable current treatment for these benign tumors is photodynamic therapy (PDT). In cases unresponsive to PDT, radiation therapy (e.g. brachytherapy or external beam radiation) may be employed. Small choroidal hemangiomas causing no visual symptoms may be observed with serial fundus photographs. Q-Which of the following ocular tumors typically displays high, regular internal reflectivity and acoustic solidity on ultrasonography?

question: Which of the following ocular tumors typically displays high, regular internal reflectivity and acoustic solidity on ultrasonography?
explanation: Ultrasonography can be used to distinguish different types of posterior segment tumors. The different ultrasound characteristics of these tumors is very high yield on most board exams. Here is a summary of these characteristics: Choroidal hemangioma • Dome-shaped • Acoustic solidity • High, regular internal reflectivity. This is the result of the tumor being composed of tightly packed blood vessels thus giving it a very regular pattern on A-scan. Choroidal melanoma • Usually is smooth, dome-shaped • "Collar button" ("mushroom shape") configuration (present in <25% cases) is pathognomonic • Low-to-medium, regular internal reflectivity. Retinoblastoma • Advanced forms display high, irregular internal reflectivity. The irregularity is due to the focal areas of calcification within the tumor. Also, necrosis and hemorrhage within the tumor contribute to its internal heterogeneity. Choroidal metastases • Irregular, lumpy contour. • Medium-to-high internal reflectivity (with irregular internal structure) Q-A 21-year old man is referred to your clinic by his optometrist with the diagnosis of "rule out retinal detachment, right eye." explanation: Bilateral diffuse uveal melanocytic proliferation (BDUMP) presents with bilateral diffuse thickening of the choroid, reddish/brownish choroidal discoloration, serous retinal detachments, and cataracts. The choroidal thickening may resemble large choroidal nevi distributed throughout the fundus. This presentation is typically associated with a systemic cancer and thus a systemic workup is indicated in these patients. The presence of BDUMP is most commonly associated with tumors of the ovaries, uterus, and lung. However, BDUMP can occur with cancer of the pancreas, gallbladder, colon, and esophagus. explanation: The image above shows a hyperpigmented lesion with a vessel spanning superficially across the lesion suggesting that it is located in the deep retina or choroid. The appearance of this lesion is classic for a small choroidal nevus (diameter can be roughly inferred based on the adjacent blood vessels and is probably 0.5-1.5 disc diameters wide. The primary concern for any pigmented choroidal lesion is to ensure that it is not a melanoma. Features suggestive of melanoma rather than nevus include elevation of the lesion, width over 10 mm, overlying orange pigment clumping, adjacent sub- retinal fluid, visual symptoms from the lesion, and rapid growth on serial examinations. This lesion demonstrates none of these concerning features although if there is concern then the lesion should be followed over time with photographs to observe for rapid growth. CHRPE is, as the name suggests, a congenital lesion marked by hypertrophy of the retinal pigmented epithelium. Generally speaking it is slightly darker than a choroidal nevus and often demonstrates a central lacunae (or depigmented space within the lesion). CHRPE are virtually always benign although can very, very rarely lead to an adenocarcinoma of the RPE. When CHRPE occurs in clusters (more than 4 CHRPE or numerous bilateral CHRPE then the findings can be a harbinger of underlying familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). The phenotypic variant of FAP with extraintestinal neoplasms including desmoid tumours, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, lipomas, and CHRPE is known as “Gardner syndrome.” Choroidal melanocytomas are a rare neoplasm that are usually located immediately adjacent to the optic nerve, are virtually always benign, and are classically extremely darkly pigmented. They can very rarely undergo malignant transformation and thus are often followed with serial photos / exams. question: Which of the following fluorescein angiography (FA) hyperfluorescence patterns shows its peak intensity EARLIEST?
explanation: There are 5 major patterns of hyperfluorescence in FA: (1) leakage; (2) staining; (3) pooling; (4) transmission (window) defect; and (5) autofluorescence. Transmission (window) defect occurs due to a defect of the overlying RPE, thus allowing more normal choroidal fluorescence to be seen. Since the filling of the choroidal circulation is early, the intensity of window defect hyperfluorescence occurs the earliest. This type of hyperfluorescence fades in the late phases of the FA as the choroidal circulation is diluted with blood not containing fluorescein Which of the following is true regarding electroretinogram (ERG) testing?

question: Transmission (window) defect occurs due to a defect of the overlying RPE, thus allowing more normal choroidal fluorescence to be seen. Since the filling of the choroidal circulation is early, the intensity of window defect hyperfluorescence occurs the earliest. This type of hyperfluorescence fades in the late phases of the FA as the choroidal circulation is diluted with blood not containing fluorescein Which of the following is true regarding electroretinogram (ERG) testing?

options.D: the ERG can be used to estimate visual acuity
options.C: the macula contributes 10-15% of total photopic response
options.B: rod function can be measured by the photopic ERG
options.A: rod function can be measured by the 30-Hz flicker response

explanation: The ERG measures the mass response of the photoreceptors and cannot be used to estimate visual acuity. In fact, only 10-15% of the ERG response can be attributable to photoreceptors in the macula. Cone function can be measured with a 30-Hz flicker response since rods do not respond over 20-Hz. In addition, cone function can be measured with the photopic ERG, which is performed when the eye is in the light-adapted state. To measure rod function, one can perform an ERG with the eye in the dark-adapted state (i.e. scotopic ERG). explanation: The white dot syndromes with the worst visual prognosis are serpiginous choroidopathy (Panel C) and multifocal choroiditis and panuveitis (not depicted above). The "pseudopodial" spread of serpiginous lesions typically occurs outward from the optic disc. These lesions become atrophic over time and lead to dense corresponding scotomas. The typical treatment of serpiginous choroidopathy is with systemic immunosuppressives; though even with treatment, the visual prognosis is generally poor. explanation: All of the answer choices are examples of types of hyperfluorescence seen on FA. The OCT in this case shows a retinal pigment epithelial detachment. Pooling is marked by hyperfluorescence that increases in size and intensity progressively as dye enters a closed space (such as fluorescein leakage into a retinal pigment epithelial detachment). Once the closed space fills, the area of hyperfluorescence remains stable in size differentiating pooling from leakage. In the FA of this patient (see below), there is hyperfluorescence present early in the FA with a slow increase in intensity yet the area of hyperfluorescence does not continue to expand after reaching a maximal size. Leakage is marked by hyperfluorescence that increases in size and intensity over time corresponding to extravasation of dye from leaking blood vessels. Choroidal neovascular membranes and neovascularization are examples of lesions that leak on FA. Window defects are usually related to damage to the retinal pigment epithelium causing increased visibility of the underlying hyperfluorescent choroid. Geographic atrophy is a classic example of a lesion that exhibits window defect related hyperfluorescence. Hyperfluorescence from a window defect is usually more prominent early in the FA and declines with time corresponding to the concentration of dye in the choroid. Staining is marked by uptake of fluorescein into structures such as drusen or the optic disc. Staining causes hyperfluorescence that maintains its intensity late into the FA but without an increase in the area of hyperfluorescence over time. • Q-Which of the following molecules acts as a VEGF receptor decoy?

question: Which of the following molecules acts as a VEGF receptor decoy?
explanation: Angiogenesis is a key process by which choroidal neovascularization (CNV) occurs in macular diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Stimulators of angiogenesis include vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF); transforming growth factor alpha and beta; fibroblast growth factor families; and angiopoietin-1 and -2. A significant body of research and clinical experience supports the use of VEGF inhibitors in a variety of retinal diseases associated with neovascularization. The BCSC emphasizes knowing the specific differences among these anti-VEGF agents: • Pegaptanib (brand: Macugen). This is a RNA oligonucleotide ligand (aptamer) that binds the VEGF165 isoform with great specificity. In other words, it does not bind to all active VEGF-A isoforms. It is not used widely anymore for AMD since patients still lose vision in contrast to the newer anti-VEGF agents where significant vision gain frequently occurs. • Ranibizumab (brand: Lucentis). This is a recombinantly produced, humanized, antibody (Fab) fragment that binds VEGF. Ranibizumab inhibits the biologic activity of all active forms of VEGF-A and their active degradation products. Ranibizumab lacks a Fc region and thus avoids Fc recyling. Lack of this Fc region also makes it very small and thus allows easier penetration into the retina and faster systemic clearance. • Bevacizumab (brand: Avastin). This is a recombinant, full-length, humanized monoclonal antibody that is FDA-approved for the treatment of metastatic colorectal cancer and is used off-label for a variety of retinal conditions such as AMD. Like ranibizumab, it binds all active forms of VEGF-A. Bevacizumab has two antigen-binding domains while ranibizumab only has one. In other words, bevacizumab is much larger than ranibizumab which may lead to the former molecule lingering in the body longer. • Aflibercept (brand: Eylea). This is a soluble protein that acts as a VEGF receptor decoy ("Trap"). Eylea combines the ligand-binding elements from VEGFR1 and VEGFR2 fused to the Fc constant region of IgG. Thus, it "traps" all available VEGF with greater affinity and prevents it from binding to native VEGF receptors. Aflibercept also binds placental-like growth factor (PIGF). • The suffix of the name tells you how it works Ranibizum"ab" and Bevacizum"ab" are antibodies Afliber"cept" is a receptor analog Pegatin"ib" is a small molecule inhibitor • A 14-year-old male with mental delay comes in for a routine eye examination. explanation: Standardized tests LOVE to test the phakomatoses including tuberous sclerosis (TS). The fundus photos shown above showcase the classic findings of retinal astrocytic hamartomas which are present in 50% of patients with tuberous sclerosis and are bilateral in 30%. These are superficial retinal masses that arise from glial astrocytes in the nerve fiber layer. Below (in the explanation image) is a beautiful OCT section through a smaller astrocytic hamartoma demonstrating clearly how it arises from the retinal nerve fiber layer. Astrocytic hamartomas can be flat with indistinct margins (see green arrow below), elevated with sharply demarcated margins and a classic “mulberry” or “fish egg” appearance (see yellow arrow below), or a hybrid of the two morphologic appearances (pink arrow). These rarely if ever cause visual disability. With careful perimetry a small scotoma may be seen in the visual field corresponding to the lesion (similar to a cotton wool spot) but this would rarely be symptomatic. It is incredibly rare (case reportable) for astrocytic hamartomas to grow once they are found on exam. Just to refresh your memory, TS is caused by an autosomal dominantly inherited mutation of tumor suppressor genes TSC1 (i.e. hamartin) on chromosome 9 or TSC2 (i.e. tuberin) on chromosome 16. You have been performing serial electroretinograms (ERGs) as shown above. Based on this information, which of the following represents the best course of management?
explanation: Iron toxicity to the eye, "siderosis", causes characteristic changes in the ERG. In the early phases, there is an increased (more negative) a-wave and a normal b-wave. In more advanced phases, the b-wave amplitude becomes smaller. Eventually, siderosis may lead to total extinguishing of the ERG. Removal of a small iron foreign body is justified if the b-wave amplitude decreases. Q-Which of the following is a relative contraindication to indocyanine green angiography?

question: Which of the following is a relative contraindication to indocyanine green angiography?
explanation: Both fluorescein angiography (FA) and indocyanine green angiography (ICG) are relatively safe procedures. Mild reactions to FA including nausea, vomiting, or vasovagal reactions are estimated to occur in 10% of patients while hives occur in 1% and severe anaphylactic reactions occur in about .001% (1/100,000). Patient’s who are allergic to FA tend to have recurrent symptoms when re-exposed to fluorescein. ICG is better tolerated than FA and mild reactions including nausea or vomiting occur in less than 1%. ICG does contain iodide, however, so caution should be used in performing ICG on any patient with a prior severe allergic reaction to iodide or shellfish. Other relative contraindications to ICG include liver disease (ICG is hepatically eliminated) and metformin. There are vague reports in the literature that ICG may precipitate lactic acidosis in patients on metformin although the evidence for this is poor. To be safe, you may ask patients to stop their metformin 1-2 days prior to ICG administration. Q-Which of the following is FALSE regarding the anti-VEGF drug ranibizumab (i.e. Lucentis)?

explanation: All of the answer choices are examples of types of hyperfluorescence seen on FA. Pooling is marked by hyperfluorescence that increases in size and intensity progressively throughout the FA as dye enters a closed space (such as fluorescein leakage into a retinal pigment epithelial detachment). Once the closed space fills, the area of hyperfluorescence remains stable in size differentiating pooling from leakage. Leakage is marked by hyperfluorescence that increases in size and intensity over time corresponding to extravasation of dye from leaking blood vessels. Choroidal neovascular membranes and neovascularization are examples of lesions that leak on FA. Window defects are usually related to damage to the retinal pigment epithelium causing increased visibility of the underlying hyperfluorescent choroid. Geographic atrophy is a classic example of a lesion that exhibits window defect related hyperfluorescence. Hyperfluorescence from a window defect is usually more prominent early in the FA and declines with time corresponding to the concentration of dye in the choroid. Staining is marked by uptake of fluorescein into structures such as drusen, the optic disc, and peripapillary atrophy. Staining causes hyperfluorescence that gradually increases in intensity throughout the FA but without an increase in the area of hyperfluorescence over time. Unlike a window defect, staining remains hyperfluorescent late in the FA. This patient demonstrates prominent peripapillary atrophy that is evident on the color fundus photo where the underlying sclera can be seen through the thinned retina and absent choroid / RPE. Early in the FA, retinal vessels can be seen passing over the atrophic area with minimal hyperfluorescence. Late in the FA, however, hyperfluorescence is clearly shown in an area exactly matching the peripapillary atrophy on the color fundus photo. This is a classic picture for staining. explanation: This clinical scenario raises concern for melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR). MAR often presents acutely or subacutely with decreased visual acuity, nyctalopia, and/or photopsias. Examination of the anterior and posterior segments is often unremarkable though rare cases of vitelliform lesions have been described. Given the lack of findings on examination, ancillary testing and history form the backbone of MAR diagnosis. In this case, we are given a Caucasian middle-aged male who is presumed to spend a great deal of time outdoors given his profession. Patients with MAR may have a personal or family history of autoimmune conditions, suggesting a possible association. Formal visual field testing often reveals a central, cecocentral, or paracentral scotoma. Most importantly, ERG testing shows greater attenuation of the b-wave compared to the a-wave, typically seen on dark-adapted protocols. This is termed an electronegative response, as the negative a-wave far outweighs the typically positive b-wave; oftentimes, the b-wave does not reach the isoelectric point. The presentation of MAR may precede or follow the diagnosis of melanoma by several years. MAR is associated with cutaneous melanoma in the great majority of cases, though rare cases of uveal melanoma have been described. The entity of MAR is crucial for the ophthalmologist to keep in mind, as timely diagnosis may be life- saving. Unfortunately, there is no treatment for MAR. Several autoantibodies have been identified in patients with MAR; however, their diagnostic utility has yet to be elucidated. The patient in this case scenario should be referred to a dermatologist for skin surveillance. Understanding the differential diagnosis of an electronegative ERG assists in the diagnosis of several conditions. On an ERG, the a-wave represents the photoreceptor response, whereas the b-wave represents the bipolar cell response. As such, in MAR, it is the bipolar cells that are targeted. Any condition affecting either the inner retina as a whole or the bipolar cells will manifest an electronegative ERG response. options.B: the excitation light is 520-530 nm; fluorescein fluoresces at 465-490 nm; the barrier filter is yellow-green
options.A: the excitation light is 520-530 nm; fluorescein fluoresces at 465-490 nm; the barrier filter is blue

explanation: The basic principles of fluorescein angiography are: 1) Camera flash unit emits white light. 2) This white light is passed through a blue ("excitatory") filter which only allows blue light to enter the eye. 3) The blue light (wavelength of 465-490 nm) causes excitation of unbound fluorescein molecules which are circulating in the retinal and choroidal circulations. 4) The fluorescein molecules emit photons of light at 520-530 nm (yellow-green). 5) This emitted yellow-green light, as well as some reflected blue light, pass through a yellow-green ("barrier") filter which only allows yellow-green light to enter the camera lens. you can also think of a slit lamp exam--you shine blue light on fluorescein and it glows yellow. explanation: The FA in this question shows the "expanding-dot" pattern of dye leakage commonly seen in CSR. Although the "smoke-stack" configuration of leakage on FA is considered pathognomonic for CSR it only occurs in 10% of patients and the expanding dot pattern is actually much more common. The differential diagnosis of central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR) in an older patient includes: choroidal neovascularization (CNV) from age-related macular degeneration (AMD), serous detachments from optic pits, idiopathic polypoidal choroidal vasculopathy (PCV), and uveal effusion syndrome. Retinal hemorrhage of any kind does not typically occur with CSR and would more indicative of CNV from AMD or PCV. In many cases, findings of CSR are seen in the fellow eye including retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) changes, active sub retinal or sub-RPE fluid, or choroidal thickening on enhanced-depth OCT. question: A 26 year-old male presents for a routine eye examination. His visual acuity is 20/20 OU without correction. On fundus examination, he is discovered to have RPE mottling in the macula in both eyes. Fluorescein angiography is performed and depicted in the images provided. Which of the following is the most appropriate management option for this patient?

options.C: Focal macular photocoagulation in one or both eyes
options.B: Photodynamic therapy in one or both eyes
options.A: Anti-VEGF therapy in one or both eyes

explanation: The patient depicted in this case has central serous chorioretinopathy (CSCR). This condition is often asymptomatic and only becomes symptomatic when the fovea becomes involved. CSCR is idiopathic and frequently occurs bilaterally in males 25-50 years old. When symptomatic, a serous detachment of the subfoveal neurosensory retina is present and is often associated with a retinal pigment epithelial detachment (PED). Fluorescein angiography most commonly reveals an expansile dot of hyperfluorescence as depicted in both images of this case. A) Anti-VEGF therapy is minimally effective for CSCR when a secondary choroidal neovascular membrane is absent. The pathophysiology of CSCR is believed to be related to choriocapillaris hyperpermeability and choroidal congestion as recently demonstrated by enhanced-depth imaging (EDI) spectral domain optical coherence tomography (SD OCT) studies. There has been some recent interest in anti-VEGF therapy for chronic CSCR; however, prospective trials demonstrate low response of anti-VEGF therapy when compared to PDT. B) Photodynamic therapy (PDT) at full or reduced fluence is an effective treatment option for symptomatic and vision-reducing subretinal fluid that fails to resolve after 3-4 months, especially when the leakage found on fluorescein angiography is within the central macula. Since the patient is asymptomatic and has 20/20, this option is inappropriate. C) Focal macular photocoagulation is an effective treatment option for symptomatic and vision-reducing subretinal fluid that fails to resolve after 3-4 months. This option is best when the leakage found on fluorescein angiography is not within 500 microns of the central macula. Since the patient is asymptomatic and has 20/20, this option is inappropriate. D) Observation is the best management option for all cases of asymptomatic CSCR with 20/20 visual acuity, and for most symptomatic cases with reduced visual acuity having a duration of less than 3-4 months. Spontaneous resolution occurs in approximately 90% of cases within 3-4 months. If the subretinal fluid fails to improve or worsens after 3-4 months of observation, then PDT or focal macular photocoagulation should be considered.
